subsubtopic: NEED FOR FURTHER DEFINITIONS RESPECTING SEXUAL OFFENCES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In light of the decision in the case of The Queen v. Pink Triangle Press, whereby Provincial Judge Harris dismissed a charge of obscenity because, in his words, "Parliament has failed to define immorality clearly enough so that its courts can judge what is moral and immoral as far as it affects children". I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That as the Attorney General of Canada is severing Bill C-21, the big amendment to the Code, and bringing in a separate bill by consent of the opposition in reference to the definition of "soliciting" and "public place" as to prostitution, that he therefore also produce in the same bill a new definition of "obscenity" as far as it affects children and, in particular, make it illegal for any publisher, either by photograph or by writing, to depict a child engaged in or participating in an act of masturbation, sexual intercourse, gross indecency, etc., in light of the fact that the city of Toronto has already experienced the horrible murder of a young boy by the name of Emanuel Jaques, and child obscenity in that city is still flourishing.

MEASURES TO ENSURE ADEQUATE SUPPLY OF OIL TO CANADIAN REFINERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. On at least five separate occasions in this House over the last ten days the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has attempted to calm and soothe the fears of some of us that the Iranian disruption of crude oil supplies was serious and would bring about a worldwide shortage and that due to the lack of any meaningful policies on the part of this government, Canada is particulary vulnerable.
Because of our exposure in the House yesterday with regard to the deplorable situation of Imperial Oil, the minister has now done a complete flip-flop and agreed that the situation is serious. Because the minister is now putting the heat on Exxon of the United States and Imperial Oil of Canada because of the disruption of their offshore supplies, I wonder if he can tell us what he is going to do about a similar cutoff of offshore crude supplies to the Canadian refineries of BP, Fina, Golden Eagle and Texaco all of which are suffering because of the same type of percentage cutoff which Imperial Oil at its Montreal and Dartmouth refineries is suffering.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: MEASURES TO ENSURE ADEQUATE SUPPLY OF OIL TO CANADIAN REFINERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member inadvertently misquoted my position: that is not a new tactic on his part. Hon. members will realize that I have repeatedly stated in this House that the situation is serious. Hansard will show that I have said it is a serious situation, but I have also said that it is a manageable situation. 1 believe it is manageable and I have indicated to the House why.
We have some excess oil producing capacity in the west which can be traded for offshore oil which would, therefore, take care of the eastern refineries. I have reported this to the House on numerous occasions in the last couple of weeks. What the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham does not realize is that Venezuela is a different kind of source of supply for Canada than is the Middle East. We have had a very long history of supply from Venezuela. Venezuela has been our major supplier; roughly 40 per cent of our imports come from Venezuela. 1 was in Venezuela about a month ago and at that time I sought the assurance of the Venezuela government and Petroleos de Venezuela, the national oil company of Venezuela, that they would continue to supply Canada. They gave me that assurance.
In the case of Exxon and Imperial Oil we are dealing with a very special situation because Imperial Oil gets all its oil from Venezuela. That is the difference between Imperial Oil and the other companies the hon. member mentioned. I think I would have been remiss if I had not insisted on the undertak-

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce which has to do with a meeting that has been going on for several months, with 70 nations, at Geneva in an endeavour to obtain an International Wheat

Agreement to take the place of the agreement that has been in effect since 1971.
It has been stated today that the whole negotiation has collapsed. That being so, the result is, or could be, of momentous proportions with regard to Canada's economy and the welfare of farmers generally. I would ask the minister, what is the present position? Is it a fact that the agreement is terminated? If so, is anything being done to restore, on a temporary basis, the 1971 agreement?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that the agreement discussions in Geneva have come to an end. The countries were not able to reach agreement on price levels or on a price range that would have been adequate to cover the farmers' cost of production. There is a spirit of continuing the food aid convention and also of assuring that discussions can begin again.
I should say, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian delegation did an extremely good job in trying to ensure that farmers were protected in regard to a fair return, and they were supported at all times by the producers' advisory group. It had been our position throughout that the producers' advisory group had to be satisfied with the kind of agreement we might achieve, or we would not want to enter one. I can say, of course, that in the absence of that agreement we will continue our work with exporters and others to achieve a fair return for our farmers on the world market.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my initial question is addressed to the Prime Minister. It centres on the report issued today by the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity which, as we know, is a body that was established last summer at the request of the Prime Minister. This body has disclosed that 33 per cent of our inflation over the past two years is due to the falling dollar, a subject which we have debated so often in this House. That is, 6.5 per cent of our inflation is due to the simple fact that the dollar has fallen so fast and so far.
On June 29 I asked the Prime Minister if he was aware that a local commentator had said that the cost of the falling dollar on inflation was 4 per cent. The Prime Minister on that date said he had not done the calculation. Would he tell the House, now, does he agree with the body that was set up at his own request, that in fact 33 per cent of our inflation is due to his falling dollar?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member said twice in his question that the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity was set up at my request. It was set up at the request of the provinces at a federal-provincial conference meeting. The federal government had other plans for the post-AIB monitoring period and the provinces asked us to proceed in this way through the Economic Council of Canada. That is just to set the record straight.
As far as the effect of the falling dollar on inflation is concerned, I have said, as has the Minister of Finance, that anybody who knows the situation recognizes, of course, that one of the effects of a falling dollar is to increase the cost of living in Canada, because Canada is a country which imports many things. It also has the effect of favouring our exports and, therefore, gives jobs to Canadians.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
This is so evident that I do not know why the hon. member keeps asking the question. It is conceded. If the dollar is low, it means our imports cost more and that we have to pay more for imported oil, foodstuffs and everything else.
As to its exact effect in statistical terms, calculations have been made, some of which have been given by the Minister of Finance. I do not know the exact effect in terms of the cost of

February 15, 1979
Oral Questions
living index, but I do know that it means the inflation rate is higher.
The hon. member opposite argues that we should have a 90-cent dollar. How much would the cost of living go up if we had a 90-cent dollar instead of an 84-cent dollar? It is a calculation which the hon. member can make. But it is obvious, whether it be a 90-cent dollar, an 84-cent dollar, an 85-cent dollar or an 80-cent dollar, that the cost of living is higher because of the increased cost of things imported into Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would remind the Prime Minister that Sylvia Ostry, when she announced the formation of CSIP, stated that it was done at the request of the Prime Minister of Canada. The Prime Minister states that it is now conceded that there is a cost to the falling dollar, notwithstanding the fact that in December, 1978, his Minister of Finance told me, in reply to another question, that I should welcome the falling dollar.
My final question is again to the Prime Minister. As CSIP has now said that if workers and others demand income increases to match the high rate of inflation which depreciation has caused, still higher prices and more depreciation will result, what does the Prime Minister intend to do when he speaks to the workers of this country to justify the inflation which he has inflicted upon them as a result of his faulty fiscal monetary measures which have led to the fall of the dollar?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in replying to the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), who unfortunately is not in his seat today, I am sure with good reason-

speechtext:
I did suggest for a good reason. I do not think it does credit to members opposite even to imply there is anything other than good thought behind that. Members of parliament frequently have good reason for being absent, and I am sure the hon. member does today. However, I did promise the House leader of the official opposition that 1 would have an answer today. Otherwise I would wait until the hon. member was back either from a committee meeting, some very important work in a department or his constituency, all of which members of parliament should do. As is my commitment to the House leader of the opposition, I am making my response to this question of privilege or alleged question of privilege which was raised yesterday by the hon. member for Victoria.
I have had an opportunity to review the various references which he cited. It appears that the hon. member for Victoria has either misunderstood or misinterpreted the actual facts. For the benefit of the hon. member when he reads this in Hansard, and for the benefit of other hon. members since it was suggested that the privileges of all members of the House were involved, I would like to review the sequence of events which he reviewed in such great detail yesterday.
First, the competitors for' the new fighter aircraft were required to submit their initial bids by February 1, 1978. That was done. However, while the evaluation process was under way, representations were received to provide additional time so that they could refine their original bids. The indication was that they would improve their original offers. Indeed, hon. members will recall that there were some unsolicited proposals at that time on this very important contract.
1 felt it was unfair to allow some to submit proposals and not give everyone the same opportunity. As a result of that and a cabinet decision of June 29, 1978, it was agreed to grant a period up to August 1, 1978 during which time competitors would have the opportunity to resubmit their proposals. This was deemed an acceptable time-frame for all competitors. All proposals were received by August 1 and no extension of time was requested or granted after that period.
The new proposals were evaluated by the government team and on November 23, 1978, cabinet reached a decision on the short list and I subsequently made a statement on motions before this House announcing that decision. The hon. member raised the question of Chancellor Schmidt raising this with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Indeed, it was done.
I think it is the sequence of events, the dates, which has confused the hon. member. The meeting between the Prime Minister and Chancellor Schmidt was in early July when it was requested that the period be extended. There had already been an agreement to extend that period. There was no request or agreement to extend it beyond August 1.
Everything has been on schedule since then. Therefore, I do not see how the hon. member could feel that he had been misled. Indeed, if there is reason for a question of privilege, I need only refer to the hon. member's question of privilege where he used the terms "falsehood" and "untruthful replies", which while they are not the same as the four letter words that are unparliamentary, have equally the same intent. However, I
Privilege-Mr. McKinnon
do not intend to raise a question of privilege on something like that.
I believe that when the hon. member returns and sees the sequence of events, he will realize that everything has been in order and that there was a misunderstanding of the dates involved and the sequence of events. However, it grieves me that words such as this can be used for a misunderstanding and the time of the House taken up by a question of privilege requiring a lengthy reply.
I wish further to point out that at the time of answering the hon. member's question I said, and I quote from Hansard of November 7, 1978, at page 867:
I expect to have this matter before cabinet this month, hopefully with a decision on the short list before the end of the month or early in December.
We more than met that deadline. I completed my response by saying there has been some slippage because of the length of time it takes to evaluate these new proposals. I think that was a misunderstanding. I said:
-I am looking forward to the final contracts being negotiated and the final choice being made in the new year, but not before late spring of the new year.
We are in the new year, but not yet into late spring. I stand by that. It will not be before late spring.

I am prepared to do so, of course; I do not think I should make a final determination of this matter in the absence of the hon. member. This is a simple courtesy we have always accorded and I have no difficulty in extending it in this case.
I would, however, stress the problem we get into when complaints of this kind are raised; that is, when there is some dispute with respect to replies which have been given. This is a political forum and a legitimate area, but it has been a long standing practice that answers given and statements made in the House of Commons are accepted by members. We therefore get on to dangerous ground when attempting to indicate that an answer has been inaccurate, misleading or false, things of that sort. And when the words "false" or "dishonest" and similar words are used, we enter into another procedural problem because these are unparliamentary terms. While I will reserve the complaint of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) until he is back in the House, I think I should point out that we must be very careful when entering into matters of this sort that we do so with great caution from

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: MR. CROSBIE-TELEVISION INDUSTRY-ALLEGED FALSEHOOD IN REPLY OF MINISTER OF INDUSTRY, TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter which I believe to be a breach of the privileges of members of this House. In answer to an oral question I put to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) on Tuesday, February 13, the hon. gentleman gave an answer which, as far as I can see, was false. For a member of the government to give a member of the House false information is certainly an interference with his privileges as a member in his attempt to do his duty. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I have listened to the words Your Honour has just spoken. This is the first opportunity I have had to raise the matter having regard to the necessary research involved. Although I knew on Tuesday afternoon that something was wrong about the minister's answer, it was not until this morning that I was able to contact the industry concerned and find out for sure that the information was not accurate.
I asked the minister a question about colour television sets manufactured in Canada in December. I pointed out that there was a decline of 81 per cent in December, 1978 as compared with December a year earlier. I also said that on a year to year basis sales of Canadian made colour television sets were down by 114 per cent. I asked the minister, in view of the fact that the Canadian TV manufacturing industry was disappearing, whether the government had any program to assist the industry during the present year. I asked him what action does the government intend to take. In his answer the minister mentioned the pleasure it gave him to place on the record that his department, under the enterprise development program, had specifically helped one of the major television manufacturers in Canada, namely Electrohome, and helped to put that company back on its feet.
In fact, Electrohome is not manufacturing television sets, Mr. Speaker, but I will come back to that. The minister continued:
-we were out of production of colour television sets for some time, but now Electrohome has gone into production because of the advantages due to the present value of the Canadian dollar. We are now enlarging our production of colour television sets.
He added that the increased production should show up in the statistics for 1979.
We contacted Electrohome in this connection. The fact is that there is only one company in Canada which manufactures colour television sets. There were 11 in 1973 but there is now only one significant producer, RCA. Electrohome does not produce, does not manufacture, any television sets in Canada.

In December, 1978 Electrohome received a $15 million loan from the Royal Bank under the enterprise development board arrangements and it was not for the purpose of putting them into the position to produce television sets or manufacture them. There was no such connection. This assistance was given because Electrohome was seeking to reorganize due to the collapse of the consumer electronics market, TV manufacturing and the like, which was precipitated by the government's tariff policy and what is alleged to be foreign dumping. Electrohome had to get out of the business of manufacturing TV sets in Canada because of what they allege to be the failure of government policy. They then got a loan from the government to go into other activities. That is what the loan was for, not to manufacture television sets. The fact is that they are not now manufacturing television sets. Because of the devaluation of the dollar in July they plan to begin assembling 28-inch colour TV sets in Canada. They will not manufacture them and they are not manufacturing them now.
The minister laughs. The minister is careless with the truth. He is grossly negligent about the answers he gives in the House and now he chooses to laugh. The minister is asinine. We cannot trust a word he says in the House, Mr. Speaker. He says he has helped one of the major television manufacturers in Canada, namely Electrohome. He says we were out of production of colour television sets but now Electrohome has gone into production. He says we are not producing television sets. He says we are now enlarging our production. Every one of those statements is false. Yet the minister thinks it is amusing that he should get up in the House and give us information which is inaccurate, which is false. I submit-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CROSBIE-TELEVISION INDUSTRY-ALLEGED FALSEHOOD IN REPLY OF MINISTER OF INDUSTRY, TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Order. With respect, the hon. member has now made an allegation of falsehood against a minister and has used an unparliamentary term. If he wishes to make an allegation that the minister has deliberately misled the House, he will have to stand by that allegation and make it specific so that a charge can be identified and take its proper course. If not, the allegation that the minister has said something false to the House is unparliamentary and the hon. member cannot be permitted to use that term.

subtopic: MR. CROSBIE-TELEVISION INDUSTRY-ALLEGED FALSEHOOD IN REPLY OF MINISTER OF INDUSTRY, TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: On that point, Mr. Speaker, as I understand it, Beauchesne at pages 110-112 says that since 1958 it has been parliamentary to use the expressions "false" and "falsehood". These have now been found to be parliamentary. If Your Honour says they are not parliamentary expressions I can only say that in my view the minister has given the House false information. Whether he is grossly negligent in what he says or whether he did it deliberately is not for me to say. The minister will have to explain whether he is just careless with the truth or whether he was deliberately misleading the House. I do not know. After I have heard his explanation I presume I will have to accept it, but I say a blatant falsehood was expressed in this House on Tuesday.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let us examine what is happening in the House. If members of parliament expect detailed answers to specific problems, the long standing practice has been to put them in writing on the order paper. Ministers have then taken the questions to their departments and obtained detailed answers. Many hon. members do that, but ministers should not be expected to have details at their fingertips all the time. That is quite impossible.
My answer to the hon. member is that we are helping many companies. We helped one specifically. One could have questions as to the words "manufacture" and "assemble". What is the difference? Manufacturers make component parts. An assembly plant takes component parts, whether they are made at that plant or somewhere else, and puts them into an automobile, television set or whatever. Granted, by narrow definition there is a difference between those words, but thousands of assembly plants are also manufacturing plants, and that is the interpretation I used with regard to Electrohome.
Today the hon. member admitted that the enterprise development program did help the one named company substantially. I do not think that the company will deny that. The hon. member did say today that the company is going into the business of assembling colour television sets. I said that that company is now going into the business of manufacturing colour television sets. I do not think there are many manufac-
Privilege-Mr. Crosbie
turing companies which do not reach out and obtain parts from other sources and assemble them in their own plants. The only misleading must be with regard to the difference between "assembling" and "manufacturing", and I say again that thousands of manufacturers are in a sense assemblers as well.
If the hon. member wants me to define every manufacturing plant as just an assembly plant, I do not think that is really the essence of the question. The question is whether my department helped a manufacturing plant or an assembly plant in going into the television business. Is that company going to go into the business of manufacturing or assembling colour television sets? Yes, it is, and the hon. member admits it is; so I do not know what his argument is.

subtopic: MR. CROSBIE-TELEVISION INDUSTRY-ALLEGED FALSEHOOD IN REPLY OF MINISTER OF INDUSTRY, TRADE AND COMMERCE

Order, please. I think the last sentence of the minister's procedurally concludes the matter. This is in fact an argument, as almost all these cases come to eventually, an argument or disagreement. Occasionally they do result in a discovery that somehow misleading information is given to the House, and invariably when that is done the person who is responsible indicates that it was not done deliberately and gives an explanation. That is almost the invariable result.
However, I do again caution the House that taking issue in this way with answers or making argument or refutation and getting into accusations of falsehood, deliberate misleading or dishonesty in some way raises a much more serious procedural problem than it attempts to solve. I think we have to be very careful about that.

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, February 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-37, to amend the statute law relating to income tax, to amend the Canada Pension Plan and to provide other authority for the raising of funds, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday we had a speech of about 50 minutes in length from

February 15, 1979
Income Tax
the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) introducing this bill at second reading. I have now had the opportunity to re-read it. Unfortunately it confirmed my original assessment of the speech. It was more of self-congratulation to the government than one of explanation. The purpose of the complex tax bill and many of its technical amendments should have been explained. There are some improvements in certain areas, and there are features which I should like to discuss in some detail.
I wish the Minister of Finance were in his seat. I intervened when the Chair was about to cut the minister short as he was discussing the dollar situation. I felt there was plenty of scope for that under clause 70 of Bill C-37. Rather than dealing with the particular problem, the minister went off on a scurrilous diatribe with a ragtag of political jibes. The minister attempted to justify his position by taking a shot here and there. It did nothing to advance the study of the bill. I would have thought the minister would welcome the opportunity to deal with clause 70 since it is one of the principal portions of the bill. It has nothing to do with income tax but is a procedure whereby the borrowing authority is tagged on to a bill. It is a procedure which is quite acceptable.
Last year the government tripped itself up over its own ineptitude in attempting to increase a borrowing authority in an appropriation bill under a one dollar item or some similar procedure. Of course, the Chair rejected it. Last November the government had to introduce a borrowing authority bill in which it sought authority to increase its borrowing capacity by $7 billion. Approximately four months later the government is back saying, "We have to borrow another $10 billion."
This will cause considerable discussion in the House. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) attempted to elicit a good deal of information from the Minister of Finance, and this morning we ran into a stone wall on this particular point. While we received some information to the effect that presently there is outstanding some $2 billion worth of borrowing authority under legislation which expires on March 31, 1979, there will be a further $3.8 billion worth of authority which will be valid under previous legislation. With the $7 billion sought in this bill for the fiscal year 1979-1980, there will be authority for approximately $13.8 billion. Why is this money needed?
If one looks at clause 70 of the bill, it indicates that the moneys will be required for public works and general purposes. Let us look at what may come in under public works and general purposes. Most if it will be there in case the government wants to go to the rescue of the dollar. In the past year some $5 billion has been borrowed in the foreign market. Under clause 70 the borrowings may be in foreign currencies and at various interest rates. As well they may be repayable in foreign currencies, but the loans are strictly for the purposes of the exchange fund, to maintain the Canadian dollar as a so-called floating dollar. Of course, this is a complete misnomer; it is a misrepresentation. It is not even a dirty float; it is a supported dollar. When one gets into the market to the extent

of $5 billion, there is no question that it is an active support and that the government is utilizing, in a rather vain effort to maintain the level of the Canadian dollar, whatever tools are available in a monetary sense.
The government does not have courage.
I want the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Martin) to take note of that. On the eve of an election, the Minister of Finance and this administration does not have the moral courage to tell Canadians that it will have to engage in other measures of a fiscal nature. The available choices are being discussed with the governor of the Bank of Canada, yet none of them are palatable. Goodness gracious, they will be a heck of a lot more palatable than for Canadians to see the Canadian dollar go down below 83 cents, and perhaps it will go down to 79 cents. This is not doom and gloom.
I heard all the Liberal speeches in 1962 when the dollar was going down from 95 cents to 92.5 cents. Let me assure the House that they got the wind up in the Canadian public at that time on a staged and spurious situation. This time the situation is of their own creation because of their inability to maintain confidence in the Canadian dollar. The fact the dollar is down to 83.5 cents is merely a measure of the lack of confidence in the international market and on the part of Canadians themselves.
Nonsense!

The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) would not know where to invest a $10 bill in the foreign money market. Why is it that Canadians since 1973 have been spending on a capital basis up to $700 million more in foreign markets than foreign moneys are being invested in Canada for capital purposes? Why is it that Canadian corporations are investing in the United States, buying buildings, building skyscrapers and shopping plazas?
Because they are businessmen.

Precisely. They are businessmen and they know they will receive a better rate of return in the United States. The tax on corporate profits in the United States is lower; their return is much quicker; the businessmen do not have to wait around for endless periods, as they do in Canada, attempting to get regulations passed by this board, this bureaucrat, this provincial or municipal office. It is a crazy situation which we have.
All hon. members opposite refuse to recognize the bottom line of the deficit in the current account of close to $5 billion. Perhaps there will be a commodity surplus this year, and perhaps there was one last year; but when there are service charges, dividends, travel accounts and a negative flow of capital, then there is a current account deficit. There is no pushing beyond that line. The Canadian government has to cover this deficit by borrowing abroad. It has actually reached the point now that it has to borrow to pay the interest on its loans abroad. This is the position of a bankrupt, and this is
February 15, 1979

what we are being asked to accept in clause 70. This is fully within the subject matter of this bill.
The minister did not say yesterday or this morning before the committee what he intends to do. He must come clean and be honest with the Canadian people. Mind you, to ask the minister in his present frame of mind to be honest with the Canadian people is perhaps asking too much and reaching too far. After all, we are on the eve of an election and these are the unsavoury details members on the government side would like to sweep under the rug. These are the unsavoury things that have accumulated over the past years as a result of this government's financial maladministration. This is the sort of thing that members on that side are trying to convince the Canadian people does not exist. They want to wave flags in our faces. As someone has said, try going to your banker with a flag in your hand to see how far you get. That is precisely what the Canadian public is being invited to do by this present administration.
Bonus issues are being blown entirely out of proportion. Let us look at this form from the point of view of taxation levels in this country, from the point of view of the value of the Canadian dollar, the degree of inflation and the level of unemployment. Let us see what progress there has been over the past four and a half years in this regard. Everything has gone up; unemployment has gone up from 5.1 per cent to 8.1 per cent, inflation has gone up, and now the rate of inflation is increasing. The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) should know that as the value of the Canadian dollar goes down the rate of inflation will increase. This is a fact because about 70 per cent of our imports come from the United States. We all know that it will be difficult to turn our economy around, but this fact is being played down. All these things have occurred since 1963, and those on the government side cannot duck that fact.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance talked about Canada being a great world trader. That may be; we are proud of the exports this country has managed and we are proud of the progress we have made in the way of exports. What is the situation when we take away petroleum products from that increase in exports? That is where the greatest increase has been in price and quantity.
What about pulp and paper?

Are you suggesting an increase this year over the last couple of years? The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) knows that three years ago the lumber business in British Columbia was not worth a nickel.
But now it is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: It is certainly much better now, is it not?

It is temporarily better now, but that is not progress. As a matter of fact, petroleum
Income Tax
products are declining in quantity. Our exports of these products have declined in quantity as a result of deliberate government policy.
I often wonder about the position taken by members of the NDP, particularly the leader of that party. He wants the Canadian government to restrict the export of petroleum and natural gas. Let us talk about what the governor of the Bank of Canada said the other day that $500 million could be found immediately if we increased our exports of natural gas to the United States. The governor said he was impatiently awaiting the government's favourable decision in this regard. I am paraphrasing his words, but that certainly was his attitude. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) says we should not export any natural gas; rather we should send it to Quebec City and the maritimes. That just shows how bankrupt he is in his idea about how long it takes to build a pipeline.
Who is going to pay for the cost of converting the heating units in the homes in Atlantic Canada from oil to gas? Who is going to pay for this conversion cost all the way along the river from Quebec City? Is it to be paid by the Canadian government, the Quebec government or the governments of the Atlantic provinces? Even with the best of intentions it would be five or six years before a gas distribution system could be developed in the maritime provinces and down river to Quebec City and beyond. In the interval the small gas producers in Alberta would be shut down. They would be shut down as a result of a lack of cash flow. The gas in Alberta at this time is not necessarily being produced by the big producers who can afford to wait. There are many small independent companies producing gas. They have been making this point all along. If hon. members on the government side would attend meetings addressed by representatives of the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada and the Canadian Petroleum Producers' Association, they would realize this fact.
In the past two years the Government of Canada, along with the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan, have stimulated exploration for petroleum and natural gas. This has resulted in increased flows of gas. We have provisions in this bill for the same purpose. In spite of this, members of the NDP and some government members say we should not export gas at this time. They say we should not increase flows at this time, that we should shut these wells down, and perhaps in five years we will be able to get some gas into the Atlantic provinces, providing the people there want it and are able to pay for it. That just does not make sense.
The provisions the minister has included in Bill C-37 to encourage the production of petroleum and natural gas in Alberta, Saskatchewan and elsewhere will produce more gas. I am prepared to congratulate the minister in that regard as that is one of the better features of his bill. This feature was hard to come by. It was like pulling teeth to convince this administration that this had to be done. It was only because of a tough stand taken by certain provincial governments in this regard that this occurred. Whoever it is that feels he is to be con-

February 15, 1979
Income Tax
gratulated for this, let him strain his shoulders patting his own back. This was a good decision and I unreservedly support it.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) would be the first to recognize that there is going to be an awful lot more gas available unless this industry is shut down. Many small independents are at the point of having to shut down now. No money is recovered from gas that is down a well. It may have cost $150,000 to $250,000 to drill the well, but where is the cash flow until that gas is sold? That points out the idiocy of this situation. On one side we have people saying we should shut production down and not export. No wonder they have no members in that area. They could not give away ice-cream cones to a Five year old. It makes one wonder sometimes. I know that the minister is in the House and when he closes the debate-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: Right now!

-there will have to be an explanation of this $10 billion. There will be available to the minister in fiscal 1979-80 $13.8 billion. There is the $2 billion which will expire on March 31, then there is $3.8 billion which will carry on into the next fiscal year, and he is now asking for another $10 billion.
From the budget speech we learned that there would be a cash requirement of $10.7 billion for this coming year, and that leaves a cushion of approximately $3 billion. What we want to know is what the minister's estimate is of how much of that will be required for foreign exchange borrowing. This is not an issue which the minister can sweep under the rug. We are down to the point where, as I said yesterday, in my adult lifetime I have never known the Canadian dollar to be as low as it is now.
It is no longer a case of saying, "Oh well, we'll be able to sell more and more at that lower price". That just does not wash because we buy too much, and as a result the cost of imports affects the cost of living and leads to higher inflationary rates, so the wheel turns once more. All we get is a recurring cycle but at a faster pace. It is a suicide course. There is no doubt that at some point the government will have to bite the bullet and take some other measures, and there are many open for consideration. The government must take the public into its confidence and explain to it what it intends to do and for what purpose. The public has not heard a thing about this tool.
Having said that, I would like to turn to other features of this bill. The one thing which bothers me about this particular bill, and I might as well touch on it at the beginning, is the redefining of small business. To me, it smacks of a dog in the manger.
Oh, oh!

If the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) understood the effect of this, and if he came from a part of the country where

this provision applied, he would realize just what I am talking about.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He has trouble getting to work in the morning.

I refer to small business, and the definition is there. If the province of Quebec had only followed the province of Alberta in this rather salutary example, the notaries would be allowed to incorporate. I am not going to go through the process of what this means, but what is significant is that a corporation pays income tax at a lower level, based upon the limitations of small business. The owner of the small business then dr^ws his salary, upon which he pays income tax at his personal rate, and what is left may be invested.
The point which some of my constituents have made is that it gives them the choice of investing this money in, for example, an RRSP, the purchase of Canadian equities, and so on. But it is an investment made by the individual concerned. There are many people on the other side who would say, "Tax everybody to the hilt, the government will take the money and spend it as it sees fit". That is what it is saying in this bill.
I would like to know what the difference is between an architect and an engineer with regard to why they should be able or not able to incorporate. Why should a qualified insurance agent be allowed to incorporate but a notary or an individual who limits his legal practice to that of a solicitor is not allowed to incorporate? Is a dentist a naughty businessman? Is a doctor a naughty businessman? They are both professionals. There are many other professionals in business who are entitled to incorporate and therefore take the benefit of the rates. They ultimately pay tax because the accumulation of money as a result of the lower tax rate must ultimately be disbursed. In the interval, however, they have been able to invest their money.
Oh, oh!

The hon. member for York Centre is one of those who feels that the almighty state is more intelligent and better capable of investing the funds. The idea is stupid. The hon. member is not stupid, but the idea is stupid.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly; I will debate this with you all day.

The hon. member has mentioned that professionals such as doctors, lawyers, architects, dentists and so on are small businessmen too. The government also feels that these businessmen should have the benefit of this special tax incentive. Has the hon. member ever heard, in all the years he has been a member of parliament, of a doctor, lawyer, architect, or dentist risking bankruptcy in their business to build it up? Does that not indicate that the entrepreneur who takes such risks-not the doctors, lawyers, architects or dentists- needs such benefits?
February 15, 1979
The architect has always been able to do it and will continue to do so.
Oh, oh!

1 know what the abuse is because it is done in the province of Alberta, and other professionals want to get the same thing. The point is that it is a question of principle as to whether the individual or the state can better invest the funds.
It also portrays something which is prevalent in government circles, and I have noticed it for a number of years, and that is that as soon as money is earned, it must be taxed, and the state has the inalienable right to a big share. Of course, it is wrong because the individual does not exist for the benefit of the state; the state exists for the benefit of the individual. That is the difference between the Liberal party and the Progressive Conservative party and, of course, the New Democratic Party is even worse. I should be able to take my own money and invest it as I see fit.
Oh, oh!

If the hon. member could put two dimes together, I am sure he too would change his mind and say that the individual is the better judge of where his money should be invested, whether it be in Canadian industry or whatever. It is not so that the government can put money through Petro-Canada and buy Pacific Petroleums. That is fine. That is the kind of individual who would not last five seconds in Alberta or Saskatchewan, but that is where money is being made.
I am sorry the government has seen fit to take this step. Unless the government can show why it has to say to a lot of self-employed businessmen that they are going to have the benefits of the small business tax rate, many of them will never get to the top of the earnings. Remember, $750,000 is a lot of money to earn over the years. Surely if an architect is able to do that, why not an engineer?
Then we come to the insurance agent, the master plumber, the highly skilled carpenter, the tool setter; why can they not incorporate? They are all skilled men and so are the others, and that is where there should be parity. But somehow or other in the philosophy of the Canadian taxation system he who gets out and scratches is the one who will be hit hard by taxation. He is the one who will be bled. He is the one who leaves the country to go elsewhere. I have been told this by businessmen from one end of the country to the other. He who is successful is driven out because as far as the state is concerned he is the chicken to be plucked. He is the one with the guts, the ability and the persistence to get out and do something, and he is the one to be taken.
This act is a classic example of this philosophy. I suppose I could take a shot at those who would inspire this within the public service. They do not have the same opportunity as businessmen. These people are on salary. Therefore, no one
Income Tax
can be any better than they can. So there is great inspiration by those people, at least I suspect there is. For example, there are accountants, doctors, dentists and lawyers in government service who are not at all averse to seeing this provision in the act which will deny to those in private practice and business the opportunity of being able to switch around and defer tax. After all, he who is in the public service has the privilege of an indexed pension. But the businessman has not. Surely he should have the opportunity to put aside something of what he has earned in a place where it can grow. II there is inflation this investment will grow with inflation; I will not deny that. Why should he be reduced to a position where he cannot avail himself of that which is given to so many others? I would like to question those who are on salary and those who would propose this particular action as to what was behind their motivation. I guarantee that many of them would admit it is because of the premise: "I cannot do it, therefore he cannot do it".
Let us go through the ways and means motion. I want to give a brief overview of the act. My colleagues, of course, will spend a good deal of time on the detail of this. Then we will be in committee of the whole where perhaps we will get more answers.
In the budget papers for November 16, 1978, in the section headed "Notice of Ways and Means Motion", No. 7 reads:
Interest and Taxes on Land
(7) That the Act be amended to permit a deduction for interest and property taxes incurred after November 16, 1978 with respect to land held primarily for the purpose of resale or development by a taxpayer in the ordinary course of his business.
Of course, this is right. It is an expense of doing business. Why should the individual be denied? After all, it was denied to him in order to try to stimulate movement of land so that it would not be held in the hands of developers. What happened was predictable. Every cent of tax and interest which the developer had to pay was merely added on to the sale price. The chap who is buying, that dear old sucker, the member of the public, the consumer, was the one who had to pay. Taxes and interest were added on to the price of the land and he was the one who had to pay. This all too often happens. It is said: "We are trying to protect the consumer; we are going to add on some costs; we are going to do this and we are going to do that." Then we hear the cry: "More controls". This is just like capital gains on the sale of land. The consumer or the ultimate purchaser is the one who pays that much more and everyone thinks he has been very smart. Instead he has been rather stupid.
There have been changes with respect to restricted farm losses and that is good. There have been changes to the research allowance. Here I must say the government has finally opened its ears and listened. It has accepted the fact that there must be inducements for expenses in research, not for the big international firms but for small firms. Unless they get this inducement, research will not be done.
The benefit of research is not only for the firm concerned or for the value of the product; research means the employment

February 15, 1979
Income Tax
of hundreds and thousands of highly skilled people, young men and women-and also many not so young-who have been educated in Canada, and elsewhere often at our expense, to become highly trained in the scientific fields. There is not one nickel's worth of value in any program of scientific training unless it will be used. It must be used in research, either pure or applied. In this particular instance we are seeing attention or encouragement given to applied research. I think the Minister of Finance has to be congratulated for this hesitant step he is taking. It may be that as a result of experience over the next year or two or three allowances will have to be increased. This is something that is borne out only by experience. In any event, it is a step in the right direction.
Clause 17, which comes under the heading of unemployment insurance benefit repayments, is a rather curious provision. I do not reject the provision at all. 1 do not know why it is made a general rule, but it reads:
That for the 1979 and subsequent taxation years,
(a)	the benefit repayment of an unemployment insurance claimant be deductible in computing the taxable income of the claimant for the taxation year to which the benefit repayment relates, and
(b)	such benefit repayment not be deductible in computing the claimant's income for the taxation year in which it is paid-
In other words, if in 1977 an individual became entitled to an unemployment insurance repayment but for some reason or other it was held up and paid only in 1978, it shall not be taxable in 1978 but in 1977. I think that is correct. I would like to have seen the minister go one step further. This is of benefit to those in the public service. The negotiation of contracts in the public service is a lengthy procedure. Ultimately there may be an agreement or an award with a great deal of retroactivity. However, moneys paid on a retroactive basis are not attributable to the tax year for which they are being allowed; they fall into income at the time of payment. Many public servants are therefore doubly penalized. As a result of that retroactive amount falling into the last taxation year as a lump sum, the marginal rate will have gone up. Therefore, a good part of the retroactive benefit is lost.
We can adjust taxation back and forth. There is absolutely no reason why a retroactive salary award cannot be apportioned over the period for which it is awarded. It may go back two taxation years. It is not unknown in the public service to go into three taxation periods, and should be adjusted on that basis. I suppose it is a matter of administrative expediency that the moneys shall be collected when paid, not when they were earned.
When an award is made either by negotiation, an arbitration tribunal or someone else, surely it should be spread over the period concerned. If this is recognized with regard to unemployment insurance benefits and the allocation of premiums, it should be recognized with regard to wages and salaries and any increments arising therefrom. I again quote:
Canadian Exploration Expense 
(19) That the provisions of the Act permitting the deduction of Canadian exploration expenses incurred before July, 1979 by individuals and non-principal-business corporations be extended to expenses incurred before 1982.
Why not all the way? Why are we so hesitant about getting rid of the principal occupation rule? During the fifties and sixties it operated to the disadvantage of those in western Canada when we were at a competitive disadvantage with Americans who came into the independent oil fields and took away the whole business, just like one would take candy from a child. Canadians were halted by an old-fashioned, out of date concept with regard to oil and gas. It is finally recognized that 100 per cent of expenses in so far as Canadian exploration is concerned in petroleum and natural gas fields can be deducted by individuals and non-principal-business corporations.
Why does this only take effect in 1982? Why is the government grudging for three years? Is it because they cannot get rid of that vestige? Is it something to be begrudged? Again it is the concept of people who do not understand the value of getting out and doing something. Then there is this provision:
(21) That
(a)	the definitions of Canadian development expense and Canadian exploration expense be clarified to ensure that, for taxation years ending after May 6, 1974, they include the expense of completing an oil or gas well in Canada, and
(b)	The definition of Canadian development expense be extended to include expenses relating to the recompletion of an oil or gas well in Canada incurred after November 16, 1978.
That is of advantage. It is good.
Storage Rights
(24) That, after November 16, 1978, a right, licence or privilege to store petroleum, natural gas or other related hydrocarbons be included in the definition of Canadian resource property.
Resolution No. 25, exploration and development expenses, is certainly good. I do not like what is said about the limitations on small business. I wonder what pressures the provincial governments were able to put on the federal government to get into this field.
There are a number of other resolutions, numbering into the seventies. I will not read them all. I think I said enough to cover what should be said at this stage of the reading of this bill. My colleagues will go into other fields. Many of the points included in the ways and means motion are pure housekeeping, plugging holes and clarifying situations which regard to the Income Tax Act.
Possibly some of the most uninteresting drudgery in parliament is amending the Income Tax Act, unless there is something that will really hit us hard. There are some small amendments that are of great benefit to the Canadian public. The individual worker has his allowance increased from $250 to $500. Perhaps there is some difficulty there determining what is that working expense. In any event, it was coming to the worker. After all, there has been more than 100 per cent inflation since the provision was put into the act some years ago. Therefore, it is only a catching up to what is known as a worker expense.
There are some inequities with regard to worker expenses, moving expenses and proposals to tax some of the benefits given to workers. For example, railways, airlines and others
February 15, 1979

issue travel passes as part and parcel of salary and retirement benefits. These may be taxed as a benefit. If the government is going to get into that, 1 just wonder whether it will get into the price of meals in factory cafeterias that are sold at the break-even point. Is that not a benefit to the individual?
Are we going to tax the individual all the way through for all the benefits he receives? Some are already suggesting, as someone was last week, that travel arrangements and the issuing of passes to members of parliament and members of legislatures should be a taxable benefit. Of course, that is nonsense because it means I would be taxed twice as much as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) with regard to that part of my income; he has to travel to Winnipeg and 1 travel to Edmonton, double the distance. As far as Air Canada is concerned, this is an allowance paid by the Government of Canada for me to get to my home, which is twice as far away as that of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. However, I would be taxed maybe two or three notches above him. I know he would not mind that as an individual, but I do not think that I should be taxed less than members from British Columbia or more than those members from the city of Ottawa who do not get any passes for air travel at all. It should not work out that way.
I am wondering about another area from a social point of view. It arose during consideration of Bill C-8, I think it was, with regard to family allowances and the question of taxation. There was a grouping of family income to arrive at $18,000-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Bill C-10.

I thank the hon. member for giving me the correct number. That is a concept of joint family income. It seems to me high time that someone here, either a committee of this House or a joint committee of this House and the other place, should look into the advantages and disadvantages of a joint family income tax return. I have in mind returns by the husband and wife or in the names of a male and female who live as husband and wife. It is time to recognize such a partnership even though it does not have, shall we say, the official status of a marriage. Under the Income Tax Act there are any number of instances where there is a penalty attached to being married which does not apply to concubinage.
How?

I know the hon. member may feel he gets all the benefits. But if he is a doctor or a lawyer, for instance, he cannot pay his wife for her work as a secretary. He could, though, if the personal corporation were continued. That is one of the advantages of the personal corporation. A bricklayer, a plumber, a truck driver, a plasterer or a carpenter working on his own cannot employ his wife to look after the office or as receptionist for his small firm. He cannot employ his wife if he is in partnership with someone else either. The firm has to be incorporated before the expendi-
Income Tax
ture can be charged to the business and paid to her. The same applies to a wife working in a small restaurant operated by a husband. This is why one often finds the wife of a restaurant operator working for another restaurant operator, simply because it is more expensive under the Income Tax Act to function as legally married than it is in concubinage.
This leads to one conclusion. We ought to reconsider this aspect of the law, and it seems to me it could be put into the chapter of the pros and cons of filing general income tax returns between husband and wife. This is done in California. I know there is a great fear of income splitting, but that could be monitored just like everything else. It would remove these anomalies which exist under the Family Allowances Act or with regard to payments under the negative income tax. It would also eliminate anomalies as far as elderly persons are concerned. Here is a classic example: a special supplement is now payable to senior citizens where there is an income deficiency. If two people do not happen to be married, they can both collect a benefit; but if they happen to be married, only one of them can get it. I think this is a totally unjustified penalty imposed on those who are legally married.
In due course this bill will be given second reading. Its progress will depend on the answers we get from the Minister of Finance. I can assure him on a personal basis that I regretted that last ten minutes of his speech yesterday because it will make the passage of this bill much more difficult; his comments certainly opened up the scope of this debate far beyond the income tax issue. I do not think it was worthy of the minister and I hope he will not try dealing with a bill in that way again; it will be the last time he will put one through in any event.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) provided another example of the government's fundamental economic policy- do as little as possible while talking loudly about how good life is in Canada. This last budget, like those that preceded it, guarantees that our economy's weakness will continue without hope of a new direction. The same poverty of ideas and wealth of blustering was well exhibited by the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau's) last August 1 pronouncement. He pledged to do all in Canada's power to achieve growth in the order of 5 per cent for 1978, yet his method offered only a warmed-over version of Tory spending restraint, restraint which has to cost the economy many thousands of jobs.
We have not achieved the Prime Minister's August growth target, nor have we achieved the finance minister's forecast of growth in 1978. The November 1978 budget was accompanied by a new set of optimistic forecasts from the minister, but other forecasters, both in Canada and elsewhere, have taken the wise step of ignoring the minister and making their own, much less optimistic and more realistic predictions about the Canadian economy in 1979.
The weakness of this government and the lack of confidence created by the government's economic record are apparent for all to see in the dollar's performance. The minister tried to deal with that aspect yesterday and I want to spend a few
3272

February 15, 1979
Income Tax
minutes discussing the reasons for the present weakness of the dollar. We have to ask ourselves why the dollar is weak. It is weak because the economy is weak. We have unemployment, inflation, unused industrial capacity and unsolved constitutional problems. Other countries do not know who is going to be in charge of this country. They do not know what our tariff structure is going to be. They do not know who is going to be in charge of our resources, and they show that they do not know where we are going by marking our dollar down. Because people in Canada and in other countries believe that our economy is weak, they are speculating in Canadian dollars by selling them. This is probably reducing the value of the Canadian dollar by between six cents and seven cents.
The government has no policy with respect to unemployment or prices. The government has no plans for the future which it can announce, so people are afraid, and rumours about gimmicks such as exchange controls or temporary surtaxes on imported goods-which would be illegal under the GATT agreement-abound. Spokesmen for the Conservative party propose those kinds of gimmicks. If we want a stronger dollar, we have to convince the world that we will have full employment in the near future and that we will have an industrial strategy which will encourage a modernized and technologically efficient manufacturing industry.
The budget speech some months ago and yesterday's speech by the Minister of Finance did not even set out goals of that nature. The minister should by now realize that the economy does not change just because he says it will. However, in his speech yesterday the Minister of Finance did outline objectives which he hopes to achieve with his budget and with his bill. Upon close examination those objectives turn out to be as hollow as many of his earlier statements.
One objective which the minister proposed was, and I quote, "to maintain and accelerate growth and demand through fiscal stimulus". Consumer demand is not likely to increase substantially as long as the Prime Minister and other cabinet members successfully keep increases in wage rates lower than increases in the consumer price index, yet that is a deliberate well thought-out but wrongful policy objective of the government.
In the third quarter of 1978 real consumer spending grew only by less than 1 per cent, despite stimulative retail sales tax cuts, which the government has neither renewed nor increased. Current forecasts such as that of the Financial Post are for a consumer spending increase of about 3 per cent, no better than the last two years and much worse than the 5 per cent to 8 per cent gains of 1971 to 1976.
Another stated objective of the budget is to put downward pressure on prices and costs, yet the Minister of Finance has already abandoned his goal here. In November he predicted an inflation rate of 6.5 per cent, but this month before the Canadian Club of Toronto he changed his forecast to 7.5 per cent, undercutting the thrust of the budget and confirming the forecast of the Conference Board that inflation will remain in the 8 per cent range, if it does not go even higher. The budget
[Mr. Orlikow.J
is supposed to stimulate capital spending, but as I shall show later, it is more likely just to stimulate corporate profits.
Research and development is also supposed to be stimulated, but even the Canadian Manufacturers' Association estimates that only $50 million more industrial research and development will be produced, when increases of more than $250 million a year would be required to meet the government's own target in this field.
Another objective of the budget is stated to be assistance in overcoming the structural problems of sectors of the economy, yet the effectiveness of such measures is surely undercut by the minister's rejection of an industrial strategy for the country. Every industry and every plant gains from this tax measure, regardless of need and of who will benefit.
Similarly, the attempt to use across the board tax breaks to support regional development cannot hope to succeed as long as there is no specific industrial strategy with realistic goals and measures to tackle the structural weakness of the economy in poor regions. Every study of the Atlantic region proves conclusively that despite the hundreds of millions of dollars poured in through regional economic expansion development grants, relative earnings of people in the Atlantic provinces as compared with Ontario have not changed at all.
The minister now admits publicly that most economic forecasts of the growth rate in 1979 are, and I quote, "considerably less than 4 per cent", yet this budget adds up to zero impact on the economy at a time when the country needs economic leadership rather than another year of paralysis at the top.
The minister's November prediction of growth was between 4 per cent and 4.5 per cent. This should be compared with forecasts in the order of 2.2 per cent by Pitfield, MacKay, Ross and Wood Gundy, and 3 per cent according to the Financial Post and the Chase Manhattan Bank. The most optimistic private sector forecasts are in the order of 3.4 per cent, the optimists being Dominion Securities and the Conference Board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext: And OECD.

It is little wonder, therefore, that yesterday the minister did not repeat any forecasts of economic growth in 1979. Even he must be coming to realize that the budget is having no impact on the economy. The only real tax cut in the budget, the increased deduction for employment expenses, will give the average taxpayer less than a dollar a week more to spend. This will not help meet the rising cost of living, nor will it generate the growth in consumer spending needed if we are to start creating jobs for the unemployed.
Over-all, the level of stimulus contained in the budget does not even undo the damage resulting from the August 1 cutbacks. The government admits this in the budget when it forecasts the number of new jobs in the coming year will be 200,000 less than the number claimed for 1978. I suggest that the minister study the long article in this week's Financial Times before he boasts about the supposed number of jobs
February 15, 1979

created last year. There is no question that the economy needs a major stimulus. This budget and this bill fail to provide that stimulus. The reduction in the manufacturers' sales tax would have been a positive step if the government had taken steps to ensure that the reduction was passed on quickly to consumers rather than issuing polite, begging requests for business to pass on the tax cut and endlessly promising to look into the situation.
We in this party have repeatedly urged the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to call in the major companies which have raised their prices so markedly, despite record profits, and to warn them that they ought not to do it or else there will be legislation to stop those practices. President Kennedy did that with success, President Johnson did that with success, but this government refuses to take even those gentle steps. Still, the major personal tax reduction and the major program of public investment which are also needed to turn the economy around are totally lacking in this government's thinking.
The lack of stimulus from the budget is seen in the continuing stream of forecasts about a slower rate of growth in 1979 than we had last year. It can be seen in the recent call by the Financial Times for a new budget only three months after the November effort which is embodied in this bill. That editorial in the Financial Times stated, and I quote:
The world is not unfolding as Finance Minister Jean Chretien expected three months ago and the finance department should be preparing a revised budget to deal with the changing situation.
After noting the signs of a new economic downturn and the irresponsible attitude of the Tory and Liberal discussion of economic issues, the editorial continues, and I quote:
The deficit is a phoney issue. The real issue ... is what they can do to get the country out of the present stagflation swamp and the seemingly endless succession of years in which growth is a meagre two or three or four percent.. . Chretien's new and higher estimate of inflation this year, with its predictable effects in reducing consumer demand and raising the personal savings rate, makes an adjustment in economic policy urgent. A budget with cuts in personal income taxes should be brought down, and it should be produced before the election.
I want to remind hon. members that that quotation is from an editorial in the Financial Times, certainly not one of the most radical journals of opinion in this country.
One group which continues to feel the brunt of the Liberal-Tory economic philosophy the most is the unemployed. This is the second winter in a row when more than a million Canadians will be out of work, according to the official statistics which omit the hundreds of thousands of hidden unemployed. Government officials may try to talk about the present seasonally adjusted unemployment rate of 8.1 per cent as being positive, but they should try talking to the people who are out of work and cannot find another job. Last month the unemployment rate, seasonally adjusted, was 17.7 per cent for young people aged 15 to 19 years. They are going through harsh experiences at the hands of the low growth fiscal policies of this government, and the experience will stay with them for the rest of their working lives. I would point out to members
Income Tax
that they are among the best educated, highly trained young people we have ever had in this country, and they want to work. They do not want to be unemployed.
Another problem with which the November budget did not deal was inflation, yet across the country millions of working and unemployed Canadians are forced to watch their income being eaten away by price increases. The solution of the Minister of Finance is to ask people to put up with the high cost of food. He has suddenly realized that there is not much he can do about the cost of food and certainly very little he can do, if anything, about the cost of imported food. That is precisely what we told members of the House and members of the government when they brought forward their co-called wage and price anti-inflation program in 1975. The minister offers the people of Canada the hope of a stronger economy in the future as compensation for a shrinking food dollar. Well, the value of the minister's previous predictions of a rosy future shows that it is no compensation at all.
The dire situation of people living on low and fixed incomes was well illustrated recently in the Winnipeg Tribune. It was reported that one retired couple had to tell the gas company: "We just can't pay the high heating bill. We have to cut down on the food or cut down on heat." What a commentary that is on the way the system is working at present! In the past five years, the price of gas has increased two and a half times in Winnipeg, and it was up 16.5 per cent last year alone. Electricity just went up 15 per cent and phone rates are going to increase by 20 per cent in April. Yet rates are lower in Manitoba than in most of the other provinces.
Those basic needs of life are increasing at the same time as inflation of food prices is entering a second year of astronomical heights. The AIB reported that food prices went up an average of 19 per cent in 1978, and already there are predictions that in 1979 the price of a pound of hamburger will exceed $2. The days when the ordinary person can occasionally buy a steak are long gone. Those food prices increased no matter how often the minister last year tried to talk food prices down, and of course to blame the increases on the supposed crying on this side of the House.
His April, 1978 budget included a forecast of 7 per cent inflation. My colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan), and I told him then that inflation would be between 8 per cent and 9 per cent, yet he chose to continue making unrealistic predictions which both undermined confidence in the government's economic management and offered an excuse for the government's failure to deal seriously with inflation. His unrealistic predictions about inflation next year will have exactly the same effect.
Indeed, the government has been so preoccupied with adopting the Tory restraint philosophy measures that it contributed to the inflation of food costs by removing subsidies from bread and milk. The director of the Montreal Diet Dispensary, Agnes Higgins-incidentally, an organization which has performed yeoman's service on behalf of the ordinary citizens of Montreal-has said that the price increase of staples, particu-

larly bread and milk, are seriously affecting low income families. She said:
There are no substitutes for these foods. Once they go up, they never come down, and they cover most of the nutrition needed by children.
Let us look at the problem of providing housing for people. Housing is a major factor in the living costs of most Canadians. The cost of purchasing a home has gone up steadily and relentlessly in recent years. On Tuesday of this week my colleague, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), pointed out to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) that the price of rough cut spruce plywood had risen from $185 per 1,000 board feet in January of 1978 to $245 in January of 1979. In the same period, two by fours rose from $195 to $265, and that in a year when the profits of the wood products industry rose by 87 per cent.
When the minister was pressed to take some action to stop this unconscionable rip-off of the Canadian people, what was his reply? Well, he questioned the figures, which came from such reliable and disinterested publications as the Globe and Mail and the Financial Post, and he promised to refer the matter to the director of investigations under the Combines Investigation Act. This is not a criticism of the director of investigations. The government has delayed so long in bringing forward and passing serious anti-combines legislation that not only will it take him two or three years to make a finding, but when he does it, unless we have adequate legislation, he will not be able to do anything about it. So we know that the cost of housing will continue to escalate because the government simply refuses to take any real action.
The budget and this bill may ignore the plight of the low income earners, but the government's corporate friends were, as usual, taken care of. The need for that kind of friendly attention is demonstrated by the 22.8 per cent increase in corporate profits in the third quarter of 1978, which contributed to profit gains of 25.6 per cent for the full year, according to the Globe and Mail survey. That was permitted and encouraged by the same government which is trying to force working people to accept wage increases of just 6 per cent when the cost of living is going up by 8.5 per cent. Companies and the government say that this just compensates for poor profits in earlier years, yet profits fell only once in the past five years, a 5.2 per cent decrease in 1975, and that was more than compensated for in other years. Profits increased 20 per cent in 1974 and 46.4 per cent in 1973. Only one of the major banks saw its profit decrease in even one of the last five years, and large oil companies have been equally profitable. A report published by the Economic Council of Canada has documented that between 1968 and 1973 the chartered banks earned excess profits of more than $200 million, and we know that since then their profits have increased at an even faster rate.
The government's decision to keep cutting corporate taxes flies in the face of all objective evidence about the effect of such cuts. Let us just look at the record. Corporate tax concessions contained in the recent budget, which came on top of a series of corporate reductions over the past two years, have had the effect of reducing the tax load for Canadian

corporations to one of the lowest in the developed world. The background paper accompanying the budget argued that manufacturing in this country already enjoyed effective rates of 10 per cent to 12 per cent lower than those in the United States. Effective rates in the resource sector are even lower.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
