PRAIRIE FARM ASSISTANCE ACT ADMINISTRATION Mr. Gordon Towers (Red Deer) moved:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of the file or files in the possession of the Department of the Solicitor General and/or in the possession of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police relating to the investigation concerning Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to say that I am not a vindictive person; all I seek is truth and justice. Briefly I should like to outline the history of the proceedings which led to my motion for the production of papers, related to irregularities within prairie farm assistance administration during the 1974 federal election campaign.
February 15, 1979

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
For hon. members who are not familiar with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, it was established by a former minister of agriculture, the Hon. James Gardiner, to compensate farmers for crop failures due to drought, hail or otherwise. Payments were calculated according to crop yield within a specified block up to a maximum of $800 per farm. While that was the original intention of the act, the federal government has since used it to administer lower inventory for tomorrow, known as LIFT, and the grassland incentive program; the former to encourage farmers to decrease wheat production, and the latter to pay them for each acre converted from grain to grassland when the grain market was in the doldrums.
Whether or not prairie farm assistance was acceptable, the general feeling was that in some cases the administration was a political arm of the Liberal party. Prairie farm assistance employees who refused to become involved politically with the Liberal Party deserve commendation for their courage and honesty. Many who got jobs were defeated Liberal candidates or other Liberal supporters who used their positions, influence and taxpayers' money to promote the Liberal cause in western Canada. Also I was informed that in some cases applicants for positions were screened by defeated Liberal candidates, and if not approved they were not accepted. Unfortunately, some of those who passed scrutiny allowed themselves to become political tools, especially during election campaigns.
Shortly after the 1974 federal election, 1 was contacted by a prairie farm assistance field supervisor who had evidence of what he considered to be wrongdoing within that administration. My informant had instructed employees under his supervision to discontinue farm inspections during the election campaign to avoid involvement in politicking. This meant they would not be paid. An expense account submitted by a field man in my informant's territory crossed his secretary's desk. It claimed travel expenses for the period just prior to the election when he was not supposed to be on the road. The secretary noticed the sheet had been forwarded from the prairie farm assistance Regina office but had not been signed by the district supervisor. Thus she reported the error to the prairie farm assistance office in Regina. Within minutes she received a call from Regina instructing her to return the expense claim to that office immediately. In other words, the district supervisor was to be bypassed.
Even to the most naive person, such procedure would suggest something was out of order. Apparently the claimant in question was being paid for political work during the campaign out of prairie farm assistance funds made up of farmer contributions and federal tax dollars.
Had the government admitted in 1974 that in fact there was something irregular and assured the House that remedial action would be taken after an appropriate internal investigation, 1 would not have found it necessary to call in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and this prolonged uphill fight for justice would not have developed. By covering up and denying misuse of funds, despite evidence to the contrary, Canadians are left with the justifiable impression that the government does not take seriously fraudulent acts involving tax dollars.
Prairie Farm Assistance
The government prefers to waste House time in cheap insinuations unrelated to public funds, while covering up payment of tax dollars for political gain. Is there no one in that group of nobodies who would attempt to be somebody by facing up to responsibility?
The prairie farm assistance irregularity was brought up in the House first by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and myself in December 1974, without satisfactory action on the part of the federal cabinet or the then minister of agriculture. At my request later that month, two constables from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police commercial crime branch visited my office to examine prairie farm assistance documents in my possession. Subsequently the RCMP decided there was sufficient evidence of irregularities within prairie farm assistance travel expense accounts to warrant an investigation. As a result, on May 27, 1975 an information was laid against the chief of field operations for prairie farm assistance in Regina, which read in part that he;
-did by deceit, falsehood or other fraudulent means defraud the public in general and the Government of Canada of the sum of $399.78 by making or causing to be made false and fictitious travelling expense accounts and work reports contrary to section 338(1) of the Criminal Code of Canada.
I might say that the amount is small and that the person so charged must deal with his own conscience; but principle is at stake here and my purpose in this motion is to find out who instigated the false work reports and expense claims. I do not think the accused did so on his own initiative.
At the preliminary hearing on July 17, 1975, the acting judge of the magistrates' court in Regina made an order, at the request of defense counsel, banning publication of evidence taken at the hearing. During the inquiry witnesses for the Crown were belittled, verbally abused, intimidated and subjected to tactics more in line with a dictatorship than a democracy. Following the hearing the accused was committed to stand trial. Would it not have been more humane and sensible to have handled this case responsibly within the departments concerned than to force the accused employee and witnesses into court?
1 should like to put on record portions of the transcript of that hearing. This document contains questions and answers between the Crown counsel and the witness. It reads:
Q. Do you personally belong to a political party?
A. Yes, I do.
Q. What party is that?
A. That's the Liberal party.
Q. And did you back it in 1973?
A. No answer.

He told me I would be compensated.
At sittings of the District Court Judges' Criminal Court at Regina on December 2, 1975, the Attorney General's agent instructed the clerk of the court to enter a stay of proceedings.
In view of the documentary evidence of misuse of PFA funds, I asked the then minister of agriculture whether or not the employee charged with fraud had acted on his own initiative or on the instructions of another. He replied that he accepted the ruling of the court, and my legitimate question was overlooked. Court or no court, a minister should be willing to accept responsibility for an employee's performance, particularly if it is a fraudulent act within his jurisdiction.
Having been stymied by irresponsible ministers at every turn, I was forced to submit a motion for the production of correspondence, expense accounts, wage claim reports, field-
[Mr. Young.J
men's work reports, etc., between PFA employees in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan and PFA in Regina for the period May 8, 1974 to July 8, 1974.
On July 7, 1976 the parliamentary secretary to the agriculture minister informed the House that PFA records were transferred to the Public Archives when the Regina office had been closed and could be viewed there, but that internal correspondence had been destroyed. Is it not strange to have such correspondence done away with when there remains about $9 million in the PFA fund?
Having evidence in my possession of impropriety within the PFA administration, I do not need to review the records transferred to the Public Archives. I continue to wonder, as do many Canadians, why internal correspondence, no doubt in part related to fraudulent expense accounts, was destroyed. Can there be any doubt that those communications were conveniently removed to cover up illegal doings on the part of some person or persons other than the employee who was charged? The government leaves itself open to that suggestion.
When the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain asked the minister who decided to destroy the Regina office papers, as it appears in Hansard for July 8, 1976, the minister replied that the person in charge of the office, that is, the employee accused of fraud, decided that all insignificant documents should be destroyed. This House and the general public will never know their contents.
As a last resort in my quest for clarification I presented a motion to have laid before this House a copy of the contents of the file or files in the possession of the Department of the Solicitor General or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police relating to the investigation concerning Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration. I have not mentioned every approach I have made to cabinet ministers in this House to get this matter satisfactorily cleared up, but the motion being discussed now dates back to July, 1976. I believe the RCMP would be prepared to give up the documents if it could obtain the approval of the Solicitor General's department.
Thank you very much for allowing me the privilege of bringing this matter before the House at this time, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the presentation this afternoon by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers). Perhaps I should point out to the House that this is not the first time this motion has come before this parliament. It was first put on as a motion for the production of papers by the hon. member on July 13, 1976, but it did not come up for debate in the first session of this parliament.
It was again put down as a motion for the production of papers on November 17, 1976. The then parliamentary secretary to the solicitor general, my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee), replied to the hon. member that it was not possible to produce the papers he wished to see because they related to police investigative matters conducted by the RCM Police in the province of Saskatchewan under the

direction and control of the attorney general of Saskatchewan. The hon. member was told at that time that it was the attorney general of Saskatchewan who had refused to allow the production of the papers in this House. That was explained to him quite fully at that time by those who participated on this side of the House.
Notwithstanding that, the hon. member, still not satisfied although having had a fairly thorough debate during the second session of this parliament, put the matter down for the third time as a motion for the production of papers on March 16, 1978. It did not come to a debate in the third session, but it has now been put down as a motion for the production of papers as of December 6, 1978.
I cannot really give the hon. member much more of an answer than he has already received or that has been explained to him on a number of occasions. The matter was debated fully and explained during the debate which took place at the second session.
The solicitor general of the day wrote to the attorney general of Saskatchewan. Perhaps I should be technically correct and say that it was the deputy solicitor general who wrote, and permission to table the documents was refused. That information was requested by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) during the debate which took place at the second session. My colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, wrote him a letter back in July, 1977, confirming that in fact the deputy solicitor general had written to the attorney general of Saskatchewan and in turn had been told that the attorney general did not consent to the release of the papers.
In addition to that, in general terms it has not been the policy of this House at any time I am aware of that police files and investigative matters are ever released on a motion for the production of papers, simply because they could contain all sorts of assertions, allegations and things that may not as yet have been proven in court. Such a release could compromise the police in the effectiveness of their investigations, and it could make it very difficult for them to work. It might also compromise people who have come forward voluntarily to give the police information. That in a nutshell is the simple reason why these papers are not produced in this House.
I could make a number of points in explaining that to the hon. member. I could go back and quote, as my colleague did, from sources as far back as Lord Palmerston showing why in the British parliament and, through that system, this parliament, such papers are not produced. It is RCMP policy and long-standing police policy that police files are not disclosed to the House of Commons or made public in any way. The necessity for confidentiality of police reports was recognized many years ago in Great Britain, and that is supported by the fairly well-known statement of Lord Palmerston back as far as 1865, to which I have referred.
The production of confidential police reports in the House of Commons might seriously jeopardize the good administration
Prairie Farm Assistance
of justice and could seriously impair the success of future investigations of this nature. In this particular case an investigation was carried out by the RCM Police as a result of allegations of the misuse of funds under the prairie farm assistance administration in Saskatchewan in late 1974. The case was investigated and prosecuted under the jurisdiction of the attorney general of the province of Saskatchewan. The details of what took place are a matter of record and they are available to any member of this House. Obviously, the hon. member for Red Deer has those details in the transcript of the proceedings which can be obtained from the office of the attorney general of Saskatchewan. I am referring to the transcript of the proceedings at the preliminary hearing.
The alleged offence-and I stress "alleged" offence- although the matter comes under a federal statute, was considered to be of a criminal nature and the charges were laid under the Criminal Code by the attorney general of Saskatchewan. The prosecution was also conducted under the authority of the attorney general of Saskatchewan. As I have said, the concurrence of provincial authorities for the release of police investigative reports to the House of Commons has not been forthcoming.

If the hon. member for Red Deer takes issue with the fact that the case did not proceed to trial, I think he should take that up with the attorney general for Saskatchewan because the decision on whether to proceed to trial is one made by the provincial Crown who decides whether there is enough evidence. This was done notwithstanding that the magistrate at the hearing felt there might be. it is the provincial Crown's responsibility who is the agent of the attorney general of Saskatchewan and who in reviewing the case to see what he had to go on decided there was not enough evidence to proceed to trial. The evidence upon which his whole case might have stood was not there, after hearing cross-examination.
The hon. member for Red Deer said something to the effect of a court hearing that took place that would have been in the nature of something existing in a dictatorship. I find nothing of that in reading through the transcript, and I have been through all but the last few pages of it.
The transcript shows that a hearing took place, that a Crown counsel examined several witnesses, and the defence counsel cross-examined. It is an adversary system. The Crown counsel had the right and did, in a couple of cases, to re-examine witnesses. The court can only make a decision based on what witnesses say. When witnesses contradict themselves, or their testimony does not hold up, that is what a trial system is all about. Those are rights that we have fought for, not only in

this country but in others. We enjoy freedom, democracy, the right to a trial, and the right to be judged by our peers.
The examination of the witness upon whom the Crown in the preliminary hearing based its case, and the evidence which the hon. member for Red Deer seems to have adopted, broke down. It did not stand up. If the hon. member for Red Deer wanted to be fair to the people whose lives and reputations were at stake in that court case, and he wanted to be fair to all his constituents who might read the Hansard report of this debate, he might not be so selective in the questions that he pulls from the transcript. He might give those people a chance to read the whole transcript so they can then make up their minds.
Let me review the matter. An RCMP investigation was held into allegations made with respect to the possible misuse of PFAA funds. The case for the Crown consisted mainly of the evidence of one witness, a Mr. Kormendy, who worked as a field inspector for the PFAA out of Westlock, Alberta. As I have explained by reading some questions and answers from the transcript, his evidence during that preliminary hearing broke down, and in fact he extricated the accused from any criminal involvement. Notwithstanding that, the magistrate hearing the preliminary proceedings did order a commital but on review of the transcript of the preliminary hearing, agents of the attorney general for the province of Saskatchewan determined that a stay of proceedings should be entered because there was clearly insufficient evidence remaining on which to convict the accused. All the interested parties were so advised.
To conclude, I turn to the original answer which was given to the hon. member for Red Deer. "I am sorry we are not at liberty

Mr. Speaker, I think I can complete the sentence which the parliamentary secretary was going to deliver. It is the government's position that they cannot present these papers because the government of Saskatchewan refused to give them up on the grounds that this is a matter before the courts and it is not customary to give up evidence which the RCMP has collected when a citizen is on trial.
If I may, I would like to straighten out a few things. During the election campaign of 1974 certain farmers reported to me what was being said to them by men who they claimed and were, to their knowledge, to be employees of PFAA, which is a government agency. These people are not civil servants but are appointed by the minister, responsible to the minister, and can be fired by the minister. I did not take any action on these statements even though they were of highly improper and unethical political activity. To my knowledge they have never been mentioned in this House. This is one feature of this whole mess which has not been made clear. There are two parts to this problem. One is criminal fraud and one is political fraud.
Prairie Farm Assistance
When I sent word around to some of our people to take note in the event they had witnessed similar types of activities in their areas, several members of parliament reported to me that such was the case. One of them was the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), and I can name one or two of the others. When immediately after the election certain things happened that were reported to us, we recognized that they were far beyond us as ordinary members of parliament fighting a political battle, because these things were now in the area of criminal fraud.
I want to make it very clear to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General (Mr. Young) that he did not present a true statement of facts here today in relation to this case. He did not mention that every one of those employees of the PFAA had written instructions, signed by the director of PFAA, that under no circumstances were they to do anything of a business-like nature for the PFAA during the election period. They were not to do anything. When an officer is shown those instructions by his own director, that under no circumstances was any member of the PFAA to be allowed to do anything connected with PFAA work during an election period, and then to find someone doing so-called work, as the evidence quoted by the parliamentary secretary indicates and then has the nerve to submit expenses for doing something he was ordered not to do, that in itself is very close to criminal fraud. But when it is found out furthermore, and which the parliamentary secretary never reported, that supervisors immediately above the PFAA inspectors refused to sign those expense sheets because there was no authority for a person to be doing work, these people called the accused and said, "Do not worry, send it in to me and 1 will sign it." When he signed it, knowing of the existence of the director's written instructions, that is where the criminal fraud took place. He authorized the expenditure of money from the farmers' accounts to these men ostensibly doing business concerning PFA work, and when that is unauthorized, it is criminal fraud.
When the case came up for preliminary hearing the police were quite convinced the evidence they had from several witnesses-and it is very difficult to get witnesses to give evidence against themselves-was strong enough that they had a case and so took it to a preliminary hearing.
If any person reads this transcript of the preliminary hearing and reads the questions by counsel for the Crown and questions put by defence counsel, it is a wonder that the law association of that province did not disbar the bunch of them. We heard the questions by the parliamentary secretary. They were all leading questions. We have evidence of legal representations on both sides, the Crown and defence, not only being incompetent but dangerously close to something even worse, improper action.
I know what the customs are in parliament. You do not present to parliament documents that are in police custody. As the attorney general of Saskatchewan said in his letter, and I quote his words:

-I feel that it would be a breach of a confidence for me to disclose the evidence contained in statements taken by the RCM Police investigators, as these are private communications between the citizen and the police authorities, until such time as the citizen actually testifies in court.
That is the length of the protection. Why has this citizen not made his statement in court? That is what we are asking. When we turned our information over to the attorney general's department and they went in and seized the documents and took photographs of all the ones in the criminal fraud, that was only part of what we were after. The criminal fraud was a small part of the whole fraud. The big fraud was what were they doing politically. That has never been mentioned in this House, nor should it be mentioned until we get it to the proper place, the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
The first steps of the hon. member for Red Deer are obvious. As a good citizen and as a member of parliament, he turned over his information to the attorney general. He turned it over to the criminal fraud squad of the RCMP and we kept our mouths shut, all of us. When the preliminary hearing was held and all these unusually odd questions were asked by lawyers on both sides, the presiding magistrate did not state the whole case should be thrown out by the evidence of Kormendy. That is what the parliamentary secretary said today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I didn't say that.

The judge ruled there was a prima facie case and committed them to trial. There is not just one person in this who allegedly did certain things that were wrong. There are several. However, this is the first one to be tried. We are now in a situation where the police are angry because their case was not properly presented by the Crown. Who appoints the Crown prosecutor? It is the attorney general of Saskatchewan. The police are angry at the incompetence of the type of questions asked by defence counsel, and the answers. In spite of all this, the judge committed this man to trial. That answers the parliamentary secretary completely.
The judge who sat there and heard all this, if you want the ordinary layman's language of what was happening in that court, heard all these lies. He said, "There is still criminal fraud here, and I commit the man to trial."
Go back and read the papers, particularly the Regina Leader-Post. This was happening to a so-called leading citizen, one of the leading hatchet men of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan, the last dregs of the old Gardiner machine, now the new machine. There was not one mention in the Leader-Post.
When I saw mention of this in Canadian Press, the Globe and Mail, and other papers across Canada, I contacted the Leader-Post and asked why it was not covering this local story. There had been a preliminary hearing for criminal fraud and they said, "Isn't that too bad; we must get somebody on to this."
Freedom of the press.

Freedom of the press? It is a part of this whole mess we see across the aisle. When you are corrupt and using the people's money, the farmer's money in this case, to try and win an election, that is beyond criminal fraud. It is a much bigger crime.
Speak to us about 1958.

I will speak to you about anything, but you speak on your feet in your own time. I know the corruption that goes on in the hon. member's riding. The hon. member for Red Deer is frustrated because he cannot even get back from the province of Saskatchewan the documents that he put into the hands of the police. It is not only the criminal fraud. It is also the question of the political fraud. Let me add a little bit of fact to that.
Why was the director of the PFAA paid $25,000 a year to be director and not allowed into his office for a whole year prior to the election, and this man who is alleged to have committed this criminal fraud ran the organization as a subordinate? He would not let his superior into the office. When this thing hit the fire and the fat began to burn in the fall of 1974, just before Christmas, why were all the girls in the office dismissed? Parliament had voted them their salaries until the end of March. The same great fear was loose out there.
These girls had been appointed to their jobs by Mr. Gardiner, then minister of agriculture, and kept on by succeeding administrations. They did their job for nearly 30 years, close to the time of their pensions, and were suddenly dismissed arbitrarily before Christmas. I would like the evidence for that. It can only be obtained by seeing the papers requested by the hon. member for Red Deer.
I asked questions in the House of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I had warned his staff years before to watch out, that when the big boy from Saskatchewan moves in you will be holding the bag. I said that he may be the minister in charge of this organization, the PFAA, but he is not running it. It is their organization that is running it. The Minister of Agriculture paid no attention to my warnings. Now he is caught trying to explain in the House why somebody without any authority from his office went in and burned all the records. He said that some of the records were put into the archives, those that were valuable in the criminal fraud case. However, it was not the criminal fraud that was the big issue. It was the political fraud.
As I said earlier, no one has ever mentioned what the political fraud is. We know. The guys who were doing it know.
I am sure the government members would like to know. They would like to know what these guys were doing to earn this money for two weeks' work. This will only be cleared up when it is properly before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. We recognize that we will have to wait until the government changes and we can get that committee called.
Meanwhile, let us go back to the real culprit. I was concerned about this and I wrote a letter to the attorney general of Saskatchewan. It is addressed to the Hon. Roy J. Roma-now, Q.C., MLA.
February 15, 1979
A good man.

Yes, he is a good man working with Otto Lang. I will just read the last paragraph of my letter:
The public is aware of the investigation and the proceedings to date. The information we as members of the opposition had in their possession was turned over to the RCMP. A reading of the transcript of the preliminary hearing and the fact that Buchan was committed for trial by the judge raises questions in our minds as to why the Crown should ask for a stay of proceedings.
When the judge has heard the evidence, you wonder why the trial is not held. Rarely in our jurisprudence does an attorney general ever ask for a stay of proceedings when a judge has ruled there is a prima facie case. You let a judge and jury decide. It only happens as far as I know as a layman when one of the main witnesses dies, or new evidence comes up which changes the whole picture. But here we find the attorney general of Saskatchewan deciding not to go on with this trial in spite of the fact that a judge has ruled there is a case. So 1 asked him why.
Here is his answer. First of all, he deals with the request for papers. He says they have to be kept private until the citizen has testified. I agree with him. Now we come down to the part where he talks about the reason:
It is the duty of the prosecutor, notwithstanding a committal for trial, to review the evidence after the preliminary hearing to determine whether or not there is in fact a proper case to place before the trial court.
That is what the parliamentary secretary was describing:
The prosecution's allegations in this case were based entirely upon certain statements made by a Mr. John Kormendy, an accomplice-
There, Mr. Speaker, is a phrase which creates a new principle in law-you can't send a man up for trial when the evidence comes from an accomplice; that would be unfair.
Again he says this, in the next paragraph:
Further, a court in trying such a case must direct itself to the legal principle that it is unsafe to convict on the uncorroborated evidence of an accomplice.
This means that if two men rob a bank and the police catch them and one of them turns state's evidence, then according to the attorney general of Saskatchewan the other man cannot be tried if that is the only evidence, because he stands to be convicted on the evidence of an accomplice. How many lawyers have ever heard of that principle? Not many. It is brand new. The attorney general of Saskatchewan is very smart, as the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has pointed out. He is so smart he has coined a new principle-you cannot convict a person if the evidence comes from an accomplice. Well, we are not going to catch and convict many bank robbers if that is to be the rule.
The point I am making is this: what really matters in this whole picture is the fact that a citizen who is alleged to have commited a criminal act, and who was committed to trial by a judge, has not had his trial and has been prevented from going to trial by the attorney general of Saskatchewan. In explanation, the attorney general has offered a new principle of law, namely, that a person cannot be convicted through the evi-
Prairie Farm Assistance
dence of an accomplice, the accomplice being the only witness. The police are angry because there are other accomplices who want to give evidence but they cannot give evidence until trials are held. So I suggest that though in all fairness we cannot, under past precedent, give the papers dealing with the criminal trial to the hon. member for Red Deer-

Mr. Speaker, we have before us this evening a motion by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) that an order of the House do issue for a copy of the file or files relating to the investigation concerning the Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration. Even with all the good will I bear the hon. member for Red Deer-and it is considerable since we work together on the justice committee-I have to say frankly that I consider this motion an abuse of the time of the House and an abuse of the legal process in Canada.
This matter concerns the administration of justice in the province of Saskatchewan. The hon. member for Qu'appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) who has just spoken has, indeed, put the emphasis in the right place. He saw he had to contact the attorney general of Saskatchewan with respect to this matter, and he has his reply. If there is any further issue to be taken up, it should not be taken up in this House. He read excerpts from a letter of reply he has had from the attorney general of that province. I found it a little difficult to tell when the hon. member was reading from the reply and when he was interpolating his own comment, but as far as I could tell what the words of the attorney general of Saskatchewan were, he was not putting the primary emphasis for not proceeding with this case on the fact that this was evidence of an accomplice.
The fact is that the evidence which was given by the witness, Mr. John Kormendy, at the trial was so full of holes that he ended up by exonerating the accused, on one view of the evidence. It was the weakness of the evidence primarily, and only secondarily the fact that he was himself an alleged accomplice, which presumably led the attorney general of Saskatchewan to come to the conclusion he did. I am not here to defend the actions of that attorney general. I think he can well do that for himself, and he should be given the opportunity to do so if this is raised in the proper forum in Saskatchewan rather than here which, I repeat, I believe to be a wholly improper forum for discussing this matter.
I can see that, as a political matter, if there were a government of the same party in Saskatchewan, there might be a suspicion that the motivation of the attorney general was political. But that is not the case here. We are dealing with an attorney general of a New Democratic government of Saskatchewan. For a number of reasons he came to his decisions, and I think there can be no reasons other than legal ones.

Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was dealing with the effect corporate tax measures adopted in earlier years had had on our budgets.
Estimates made in 1977 indicated that since 1972 corporate tax burdens had been reduced by about $1 billion to $1.5 billion per year. The last budget reduced corporate tax burdens by about another $200 million a year.
These tax reductions have had the effect of increasing corporate profits and reducing government revenues, with the real result that the government has felt compelled to cut back on a wide range of social services. I do not have the time to enumerate those today, but members of parliament know very well what they are. There is no evidence that these tax reductions have had more than a marginal impact on capital investment or job creation. The C. D. Howe Research Institute, after examining the list of such concessions in Canada in 1976 concluded, and I quote:
Although Canada has made extensive use of business tax concessions over the years, the question of the usefulness of such measures in achieving the desired goals remains unresolved.
More direct evidence of this fact came to light in 1975 when the Department of Finance surveyed a large number of corporations to see if there had been any impact from the introduction of the accelerated two year write-off for manufacturing and processing equipment in 1972. Of those surveyed, only 32 per cent said that these concessions, estimated to be worth $2.5 billion between 1972 and 1975, had any impact on investment decisions. Only 26 per cent said they would be increasing jobs as a result of these concessions, and only 15 per cent said that they would have any impact on prices.
The most recent study, published in the November-Decem-ber issue of the Canadian Tax Journal concluded, and 1 quote:
The effectiveness of investment incentive tax policies in bringing about changes in the over-all level of investment or the timing of investment expenditures is not at all apparent.
One thing that has been apparent is the almost weekly reports of immense profit increases. Bell Canada profits in 1978 came to more than $370 million, an increase of 25 per cent over the previous year. The 1978 profits of Abitibi Paper company more than doubled their 1977 performance. This astounding increase was nearly matched by Algoma Steel, with an increase of almost 90 per cent. Consumers Glass Company did better, with an increase of about 120 per cent in its last year. Profit increases in the 20 per cent to 25 per cent range are too numerous to list here, considering that they are only average, although most workers saw their wages increase at a much slower rate of about 6.4 per cent last year.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said recently that he welcomes the huge profits being reported by most corporations operating in this country. He talks about how those profits can be used to create jobs, but before continuing to praise the profit picture the Prime Minister should consider some exam-

February 15, 1979

pies of how corporate profits have in fact been used in recent years. Those most favoured friends, the giant pulp and paper companies, have been either playing "Monopoly" with each other or investing in new operations outside the country. MacMillan Bloedel, Domtar, CP Investments, Abitibi, and Prince and Argus Corporation have all been involved in takeover bids for other companies instead of investing their profits in new plants and processes as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) have talked about.
Despite the high level of profits and world demand, Canadian pulp and paper corporations have refused to replace outdated plants or expand operations in Canada, while at the same time they expand abroad. For example, MacMillan Bloedel has committed itself, along with its partners, to pour some $131 million into a French pulp company over the next three years. It is also involved in a multimillion dollar project to develop Brazilian pulp properties, plus plywood and lumber mills in Malaysia. Domtar spent some $34.5 million to acquire a number of U.S. gypsum and wallboard mills last spring. And it is to these corporations that we are giving over $200 million to help them modernize.
The Prime Minister's assertions about the need for high profits to ensure Canadian investment is revealed as a sham by examination of the record of the government's Export Development Corporation, which is encouraging development elsewhere through guarantees of loans for new plants in other countries, plants which very often compete with Canadian plants and Canadian workers for business and jobs.
Inco benefited from Export Development Corporation loans to help it export jobs to Guatemala and Indonesia. The government's reliance upon across the board tax cuts let this corporation defer $368 million in federal taxes on 1976 and 1977 profits of $1.7 billion, although it eliminated 4,000 full time jobs in Sudbury, Ontario, and Thompson, Manitoba, in just one day in 1977. Indeed, Inco has been able to gather tax cuts and exemptions from the Tory government in Ontario and promises of the same from the Tory government in Manitoba, despite the sorry spectacle of Canadian operations being downgraded in favour of overseas investment.
What is true of the privately-owned corporations is now becoming the policy for publicly-owned corporations like the CDC. That corporation was created by an act passed in Parliament on June 9, 1971. Its purposes were:
(a)	. .. assist in the creation or development of business, resources, properties and industries of Canada;
(b)	... to expand, widen and develop opportunities for Canadians to participate in the economic development of Canada through the application of their skills and capital;
(c)	. .. to invest in the shares or securities of any corporation owning property or carrying on business related to the economic interests of Canada; and
(d)	. .. to invest in ventures or enterprises including the acquisition of property likely to benefit Canada.
How does this corporation act? CDC, which is owned between 66 per cent and 70 per cent by the federal government, has substantial investment in petrochemicals, mining,

venture capital, oil, gas, and health care. CDC companies employ over 20,000 people world-wide. One of these companies, Polysar Limited employs 3,700 workers in the Sarnia, Ontario, operations, but 6,000 people world-wide. The majority of the company's manufacturing subsidies are in Europe or the United States. In 1977 Polysar acquired a 25 per cent interest in a French plastics forming business. Polysar also operates major synthetic rubber plants in both France and Belgium.
Instead of investing money and its know-how in building plants in Canada, which could not only supply the Canadian market but which could sell on the international market, Polysar is investing increasingly its efforts and its money in corporations producing in foreign lands.
Similarly, in health care 1977 saw CDC's Connlab group acquire a quality biological facility in Swiftwater, Pennsylvania. Connlab Holdings Limited also controls 75 per cent of A/S Dumex based in Copenhagen, which in turn employs 700 Danes. Dumex is particularly involved in marketing drugs in developing countries. CDC Oil and Gas acquired a working interest in a major Louisiana property during 1977. Based in Calgary, with a total staff of 130, the Louisiana purchase cost $45 million U.S. and resulted in a 45 per cent interest in 27,000 acres of partially developed land located on the Gulf of Mexico, south west of Lake Charles, Louisiana. U.S. employment in the 14 wells, two drilling rigs and one completion unit, which are scheduled to continue for at least five years, will almost certainly exceed the Canadian based staff. With investment in Canadian oil research and exploration below par, CDC job creation in the United States is inconsistent with Bill C-219's mandate of developing the resources of Canada. The company has also bought a 25 per cent interest in a group evaluating prospects in the western approaches area of offshore Great Britain.
Is it any wonder that we do not get the kind of development which we need in Canada when publicly-owned corporations seem to be more concerned about developments outside Canada than they are in Canada?
That is the situation, and we continue it despite all the evidence that these kinds of policies have created personal suffering and have led to the economic decline resulting from this policy of spending restraints and of tax favours for the well-to-do.

It is utterly crucial to any country aspiring to industrial health that it map out and implement a strategy designed to achieve international leadership in this new wave of technology ... In apparent defiance of its plethora of human and

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak in the debate on this budget bill, partly because of the events of the last two, three or four days. One event which bothered me considerably in the last four or five days was a poll which was produced by Gallup. It indicated that Canadians did not think the economic affairs of the country were handled as well as they could have been by the government. Therefore I should like to look at the general economy of the country and also at what is happening in the energy field because these matters are related very much to the situation we are in now.
It is interesting that many Canadians feel this way, and yet many economists feel very differently. When one looks at many of the more important economists in the country and other parts of the world, one will find that they see Canada as a country doing relatively well compared to other countries, and also as doing the correct thing at this particular point. This particular budget is based upon many of these correct things.
If we attempt to understand the position we are in at the present time, it is important to go back over the last ten or 15 years and trace some of the principal points where major changes have occurred. The years 1968-1969 to approximately
1973	was a period of almost unlimited growth for the industrial world. Growth rates of 7, 8 and 9 per cent were being registered all over the world. The feeling was that this would go on forever. Along with many other governments, this government engaged in activities which years before would not be considered acceptable.
Order, please. I suggest the hon. members take their conversations behind the curtains. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) has the floor.
Right on.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The government engaged in activities which would not have been possible before this. In other words, we instituted many social security programs and schemes of this nature because we felt unlimited growth was with us. I will deal with that matter when I talk about expenditures and revenue a little later.
An event occurred in 1973 which changed the whole picture of the economies of the industrial world. Of course that was the sudden change in oil pricing brought about by the coming together of oil-producing countries under the heading of OPEC. Within a few months there was a 400 per cent increase in the cost of oil. This single factor perhaps has had more to do with the subsequent years than any other factor in this 15 or 20-year period or since the beginning of World War II.
In the period from 1974 to 1977, immediately after the OPEC increase of 400 per cent in the cost of oil, massive amounts of dollars were drained off to the OPEC countries. Last year alone there were $50 billion from the United States, $2 billion or $3 billion from Canada, and so on. In the years
1974	to 1977 the world went into a recession which was the worst in 40 years, the worst since the big depression. A recession in any country can be considered a period when there is less than a zero growth rate or a negative growth rate. Most of the major countries of the Big Seven experienced periods of recession of at least one year. Canada was the only country among the Big Seven which did not have a single year of actual recession. In other words, it did not experience one year when the growth rate was negative in the period from 1974 to 1977.
As a matter of fact, Canada's growth rate in this crucial recession period averaged 4.1 per cent. During the same period

February 15, 1979

the U.S. growth was only 2.7 per cent, and it experienced one year of a negative growth rate. Also at that time the 24 OECD countries averaged growth rates of 2.9 per cent. With the exception of Japan, our growth rate was the best. These are factors which we must consider, and they are factors which create some problems. We did not experience the same depth of recession as other countries. Because we did not experience the same recession as the United States, we had some inflationary problems which they did not have to the same degree.
If we look to this year we can see various economic groups are predicting very moderate growth rates among all major countries, the seven summit countries. Just recently a Newsweek analyst predicted that Canada would outperform growth-wise all of the other Big Seven countries except Japan. Perhaps at some other point it would be worth while to look at the Japanese situation. We could see whether Canadians are really willing and ready to adopt the kinds of measures, policies, and social styles which are being developed by the Japanese.
There is a good deal to be said about the fine performance of our country over this period of time. There was a high growth period from 1965-1966-1967 to approximately 1973. Then there was the major crash or problem caused by the 400 per cent increase in the cost of oil on the part of OPEC countries, followed by a global recession in which Canada probably fared the best of any country. Of course during this period of time there were a couple of very serious problems. One of them was the problem of inflation. It was exacerbated considerably by the fact that we had less recession than most other countries. We had considerably higher growth rates than the United States.
As I mentioned, our growth rate averaged 4.1 per cent over this period as opposed to 2.7 per cent in the United States. This created some very definite and strong inflationary pushes. In spite of a great deal of opposition at an earlier period, this was one of the reasons why the country had to institute some kind of serious anti-inflationary program by 1975. Incidentally, the program was relatively successful. It was not so successful in that the inflation rate was not brought down a great deal-it was brought down two or three percentage points- but it was successful in the sense that the inflation rate might have been a great deal higher. With labour settlements of 22 per cent in the first half of 1975 one could expect a very much greater inflationary period in 1975 and 1976, regardless of what we did in terms of controls. I think it is relatively important to understand that.
The other factor which made it very difficult for us was unemployment, but in spite of that factor we have still experienced an increased growth rate. Perhaps that is because of the initiative this created. Here again I think we are unique as a country. In all of the non-communist world we are unique in that we have had a far larger growth in the labour force than any other country. If one looks at the summit seven, the United States, Japan, France, West Germany, Britain, Italy and Canada, one will see that for every one hundred people in

the labour force in 1965, the average in the labour force in 1975 was 109, with the exception of Canada. There was an increase of roughly nine persons per 100 in the labour force over that ten-year period. Canada, on the other hand, had an increase of 46 people per hundred, or a 500 per cent greater increase than the average for those other countries.
Let us take a couple of those countries individually. The United States was the one closest to us with an increase of 28 people per 100 in the labour force in 1965. Countries such as West Germany had a negative increase, or a slight decrease in the labour force.
Such an increase in the labour force as we experienced, I contend, put tremendous pressure on the government to do many things that were inflationary, such as expenditures in respect of job creation and so on, creating in turn very heavy deficits.
In spite of this situation, in regard to employment we have achieved much growth in terms of the number of jobs. This last year we have had by far the largest growth in employment by population of any of the countries to which I refer, and we had an increase last year of over 400,000 new jobs in this country. That is a very remarkable increase.
In spite of that growth in the labour force we are finally getting to the point now, with the increase in the number of jobs, where the situation is beginning to turn in a slightly different direction. It now actually looks like we will have more job growth than we will have growth in the labour market. This is something I think that is just beginning to turn around. For a country that has had that kind of growth rate, larger than that of most other countries with the exception of Japan, we have done quite well. However, this has caused inflationary pressures because we have had more growth than other countries. Those countries were experiencing a recession, but this country, with that kind of growth in the number of new jobs, some 500 per cent higher than in any other country, has done relatively well. This is not a perfect performance, but it is relatively better than in other countries.
In ordinary times, times that we might call normal periods, perhaps the early 1960s or the late 1950s, one could adjust one's economy fairly rapidly. One could throw a couple of billion dollars into the demand side, raise interest rates, create more money, or reduce the money supply, and have some effect. I contend that with the problems facing the world today, with massive increases in energy costs, it is virtually impossible for a government to take simplistic Keynesian actions. Those were very popular, very good and well proven methods, although not always enacted at the right time. They were well proven methods for solving problems, but they have not been possible in this situation because they simply would not work. When the opposition, whether it be NDP or Tory, suggests it could go out and spend two or three more billion dollars and create a two or three-month higher deficit, or something of that order, with the expectation that we would see a massive growth in the economy, it is talking rubbish, given the nature of economic conditions in the world today.

I should like to talk a little bit about government expenditures because this is an area in respect of which I think the public feels perhaps we have been inadequate in the way we have responded to some of the problems facing us. 1 think it is important to realize that in the period leading up to 1973, or early 1974, we embarked upon a whole series of social security measures, health and welfare measures and so on, which would make it easier for the public, for the poor people and for many Canadians on old age security, to solve their problems. In this way we were giving them a better deal in pensions after retirement, and so on. These were the kinds of things in which governments were engaged. These were legitimate activities, as they are now. These were legitimate measures commensurate with the growth in the economy.
If one takes a look at two curves, that is, the expenditure curve and the revenue curve, one will see that all the way through from 1965 to 1974 the curves ran along parallel. At one time there might have been a slight deficit, and then there might have been a slight surplus but basically speaking the curves were parallel. Then in 1974, and again this has to do with the OPEC situation and the general sort of decline or recession that occurred, the expenditure curve continued on up but the revenue curve went out. That is an extremely important situation, and that is where the deficit problems started.
Incidentally, it might be interesting to note that at that time Mr. Turner in his budget, at the very strong urging of a Conservative opposition, started indexing everything and also started indexing exemptions. This was a large factor in the distortion created between the slope of those curves. In other words, we were indexing old age pensions, family allowances and a whole series of things, and in the opposite direction we were also indexing the exemptions. As a result there was a loss of revenue, and greater expenditure. At this critical time with the OPEC situation, which slowed the growth rate, and a kind of double indexing in both directions, a deficit situation was created. The policies up to that particular point had been good policies, well-formed and well within the means of the country, given the growth rate that was expected. I do not think anyone predicted the kind of changes that occurred in 1973 and early 1974.
When we look at government expenditures I think it is important that we consider how the government spends its money. The largest item is known as transfers. Some 51.7 per cent of all government dollars goes out in the form of transfers, with 22 per cent to persons, 21 per cent to other governments, provincial and municipal, and 8 per cent in terms of subsidies to railways and so on, as well as various consumer subsidies. These add up to 51 per cent, over half the budget of the Government of Canada.
The next item is public debt, which relates to wars and past expenditures. It amounts to 14 per cent of government expenditures. Then we have government operations, accounting for 34 per cent. This includes 3.4 per cent for Crown corporations in the form of subsidies, etc., 8.9 per cent for national defence, and 22 per cent for the rest of the government's operations. Taking the public debt, the servicing of debt, transfers to
(Mr. McRae.)
provinces in the form of pensions, etc., along with government subsidies, we have about 65 per cent of all government expenditures going in that direction. This leaves 35 per cent that the government actually controls, and some of this is not controlled, in the sense that it includes Crown corporations.
When a government has a deficit in the order of $12 billion it has to cut back. It is very difficult unless it cuts back in this major area which takes up to 65 per cent of the expenditures. For example, in cutting back the number of beds in hospitals in cities such as Thunder Bay, the provincial government is reacting to the very large $12 billion deficit of the federal government.
I do not wish to get into this particular aspect of the issue at this point, because it is a debate in itself, but I would mention the fact that I think governments should look at their health services and various other services which they provide, including penitentiaries, and consider whether or not there are simpler and cheaper ways of providing these services. For instance, halfway houses in the area of mental health, as I understand it, cost $30 to $50 per day per patient, whereas the cost per patient in a mental hospital is $150 per day. Chronic bed hospitals, which we need more of in our community, cost about one third of what active bed hospitals cost. These are some of the things we must look at. In other words, what we need is a shift according to the needs of the people rather than many of the institutional costs which we incur.
One factor which is being grossly overlooked by the government and by Canadians in terms of how Canada is doing as an economy-and I was pleased to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) refer to the figures in his speech yesterday-is the national debt and the fact that it has not grown in this country in terms of the gross national product. I would like to explain what I mean, because I think that it is important that Canadians understand this whole business of debt. If, for example, I owe $10,000, then in order to determine my worth and whether I can pay the debt off the person or institution loaning me the money must look at three factors. Of course there is the size of the debt, then there is the size of my assets and, thirdly, my income. It is meaningless to talk about debt unless one talks about it in these terms.
When talking about the debt of the nation, and I think that Canadians are concerned about how much debt this nation is incurring, we must talk about it in terms of these three factors-the size of the debt, the size of one's assets, and one's income. Therefore in measuring a national debt we measure in terms of net debt, as we do personal debts, that is, assets versus liabilities in terms of one's income or gross national product.
If we look at the net national debt as a fraction of the gross national product over the period of the last 20 years, we find that it fluctuates considerably. In 1952 it was in the area of 50 per cent to 51 per cent of the gross national product. In 1962, the last full year that the Conservative party was in power in this country, the gross national debt amounted to 33 per cent of the gross national product. In 1978 the gross national debt
February 15, 1979

amounted to only 18.9 per cent of the gross national product. In other words, our debt position has improved considerably since 1952. It has even improved considerably since 1962, from 33 per cent in that year to 18.9 per cent in 1978.
The fears Canadians feel for the state of the nation economically would be allayed considerably if they were made more aware of this debt ratio. Looking at the figures I have mentioned, Canadians should feel that as a nation we are doing relatively well.
Another factor which gives Canadians a great deal of concern and tends to create pessimism is the grossly undervalued Canadian dollar. This feeling tends to grow in the country as the dollar declines or stays in the area of 83 cents to 84 cents. If one is looking for a date on which events turn around-and I have referred to the period in 1973 when OPEC oil was increased by approximately 400 per cent-with regard to our devalued Canadian dollar, one must consider November 15, 1976, as the pivotal date when there was a change of government in the province of Quebec. I was in the United States just a few weeks before this event and, as I recall, we were being paid $1.02 or $1.03 for the Canadian dollar. After that date the Canadian dollar declined very rapidly. It did not fall to 85 cents, but to around 90 cents. One of the major single factors which influenced the price of the Canadian dollar on the world market, was the uncertainty as to what would happen to this country should the Levesque government prevail and should Quebec separate from the rest of Canada.
There are other factors. Some of the concerns, I believe, have been allayed considerably because of our increased productivity and our reduced unit labour costs which have been coming down at a faster rate than most of the other countries in the world. There are many factors which would actually bring the Canadian dollar back closer to 90 cents, but the single unity factor is of prime importance.
On the other hand, one of the big advantages of the lower dollar is that Canada is now able to export to other countries more competitively than it was able to, two, three or four years ago. Canada's trade has increased markedly in the last couple of years primarily due to the fact that we have an 84-cent or 85-cent dollar. Another factor which is not given the consideration I believe it should be given has to do with the Canadian entrepreneur who must sell in competition with imports. This situation has the effect, of course, of creating a 15 per cent tariff on import goods, but I do not think that we have succeeded as well as we might in competing with imports. Certainly the 85-cent dollar means that imports are that much more expensive, and Canadian entrepreneurs should be able to take advantage of that situation.
The reason why we have probably not been as successful in this area is because there is uncertainty as to how long the situation will last. Another factor may be that too many Canadian entrepreneurs are taking a larger than necessary profit instead of pushing for a larger piece of the business. This is something which should be looked into and analysed.

We know quite a bit more about the export side of things than we do about the competition of Canadian entrepreneurs versus importers. This is one of the factors that has had a salutary effect on the region from which I come. I am speaking of Thunder Bay and northwestern Ontario. Thunder Bay has one of the lowest unemployment rates in Canada, although I am never quite sure what the rate is in Thunder Bay. We can never get a good sampling from Statistics Canada because the numbers showing are so small and so we cannot get a good picture of the situation. Northwestern Ontario has a similar situation, except for a few areas like Atikokan. These are mining communities which have different problems.
Because Thunder Bay is a major port from which grain is shipped, the area is more concerned with the export trade. Because of the forest products industry where roughly 90 per cent of the produce from areas surrounding Thunder Bay is exported to the United States, the area is in good shape at the present time. The depressed dollar has been advantageous to the area and is one of the major factors for its relative affluence.
1 was in Europe last week with a group of people. We visited with people at NATO and with representatives from the European economic community. Many of us got the impression that Canada relative to most European countries was very well off. We found out that our dollar could buy a great deal more at home than it could abroad. It leads me to believe that if our dollar buys more at home than abroad there is something wrong with the price of the dollar. Either we are not moving our goods as fast as we can, or there is something artificial which is creating some difficulties with the dollar which is not really understood. Basically, Canadians on this trip felt that we were very well off relative to other countries and that basically we are moving in the right direction as far as our economy is concerned. The government and the Minister of Finance should be given credit for this general direction in which we are going.
I would like now to turn to the economy and speak about some of the problems I foresee in the energy area. As I mentioned several times during the course of my speech, the 400 per cent increase in the price of oil since 1973 has had a tremendous effect on the Canadian economy and upon the economies of all countries in the non-communist world. It seems to me that in many ways, while we had this serious dislocation in our economy where $50 billion last year was drained off in the United States for oil and where hundreds of billions of dollars have moved from one part of the world into another part and which have not been funnelled back into the demand side, it has had a bad effect on one hand and a good effect on the other.
The OPEC nations have been telling us that we and they are running out of oil. I am looking at a publication called "Energy Futures for Canadians" which was tabled in the last week or so, which enunciates the concerns we should all feel about global and national energy problems.

I have spoken in this House on many occasions about energy demand and supply. There is no question in my mind that between the years 1985 and 1990 Canada and the rest of the world will have serious problems with respect to oil supplies. The world will run out or have reduced this important resource within the next 20 or 25 years so that we will have to change our lifestyles considerably. Canada has some synthetic oils such as syncrude, and the heavy oils, but basically the world's oil supply, as we know it, will be reduced within the next 25 or 30 years, so we will have to depend to a much greater extent on other forms of energy.
Canada should be looking much more carefully at how we will get along without oil. We have been reminded once again by Iran, one of the OPEC countries, that this problem exists. I do not know how many reminders we must get to realize that we are going to be in trouble. With Iran supplying 10 per cent of the western nations' oil supply which is now cut off, and with yesterday's announcement by Exxon that they would divert 25 per cent of the oil from Venezuela to the United States and other markets which Imperial Oil was getting, we are reminded again of a long-term problem which is rapidly becoming short-term.
I was most upset when we had these revelations about cutbacks that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) last night spoke about in Calgary, strongly supporting the very provincial, local views of the premier of the province of Alberta when he talked about the province of Alberta controlling almost totally the oil and energy resources of that wealthy province. The day is going to come when Alberta oil will no longer be there. We may have syncrude and so on. And the day is rapidly approaching when oil will be no longer supplied from Iran, and there will be a shortage of oil coming from Venezuela.
This is not the time for this country to become a group of balkanized provinces, with the resources of this country limited to the people in one province. I think this next election has got to be fought on the basis of whether we will be one country or nine or ten or eleven countries.
Hear, hear!

The crux of the whole matter, whether we like it or not, will be in the energy area. We have to pool all our resources as a nation. We cannot allow Alberta to control the whole thing. I worry a great deal when the Leader of the Opposition says that each province should control its own resources totally.
We have a long-term problem in this area, Mr. Speaker. All Canadians have to share the nation's wealth and its problems. This country is a cold country in the winter. Its citizens must be supplied with some form of heat for their well-being, so we must ensure that all Canadians are fairly looked after.
In conclusion I would like to say that at a time when there is no simple answer, at a time when most governments of the world face high inflation and high unemployment, problems which cannot be solved by Keynesian methods, by increasing money supply or by increasing demand, at a time when there

are massive increases in energy costs, which are prime factors in any industrial state, Canadians should look around them to see that this country has not done that badly. In spite of recession, we have had a growth rate during the last three years perhaps second only to Japan. And to compare the growth rates of Canada and the United States, these were 4.1 versus 2.7. We have done relatively well. During this period we had a 500 per cent greater increase in the labour force than any of these countries. Considering this massive problem alone, Canadians should not be disappointed in our performance. There are no simple answers like there used to be. This government has made some mistakes, as have all governments, but on balance we have done rather well.
I would like to go into the election that will be held some time in the next few months, with Canadians knowing that their economy is in relatively good hands. Their concern today should be where we are going in the future and whether we can solve some of the problems, such as the energy problem, as a total nation, or break up into ten or more countries.

Mr. Speaker, in joining in the debate on the bill before us tonight, Bill C-37, I will speak in relatively non-partisan terms because, the issues that 1 wish to raise are of such a serious nature that it is time that this House came to its senses. There are three matters in particular that I would like to deal with in connection with Bill C-37. Before doing so, I first want to emphasize that what my colleague from Edmonton West Mr. Lambert) said earlier today and yesterday, I reiterate.
We believe there are portions of Bill C-37 that are good, that should be commended and endorsed by the Canadian public. I refer, for example, to certain incentives that have been given to the petroleum industry in the earnest hope that that industry will once again become more and more a Canadian-owned industry. We endorse that. We endorse various other caretaking changes that have been made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to streamline the act and, above all, make it more equitable as far as income tax burdens are concerned.
I am not going to speak for long tonight. My first point deals with the provisions in this bill touching on the taxation of small business corporations. Frankly, we find it rather remarkable that the minister has asked us, first in his budget, then in his ways and mean motions, and now in this bill, to accept a concept where the smallest of small businesses will have to bear a higher tax load than those that are not so small. That surely is not equitable. Some of my colleagues will dwell more fully on that.
We are the First to agree that there are loopholes in the existing act. There may have been tax avoidance schemes worked out whereby those that rightfully should be paying higher taxes have been able to avoid those taxes. We on this side of the House say, identify those loopholes and plug them, but whatever you do, do not, through faulty draftsmanship or for other reasons, catch a lot of innocent small business people
February 15, 1979

who deserve a break as far as income tax is concerned but are going to be denied that break should this bill ever see the life that the Minister of Finance suggests parliament should give it. More about that later.
The second point is that we emphasize that all members of this House should think in a serious way of the implications of what the Minister of Finance is proposing. This is perhaps the first time, certainly in Canadian history, that a minister of finance has proposed that future taxation of this country be handled by regulation. Read the provisions of this bill and you will find that the definition as to who fits in and who does not fit in as a small business is to be defined by regulation. That should be the prerogative of this parliament, not of some civil servant who decides who should be taxed and who should not. More about that later.
Probably the most alarming part of this bill is the last clause. I refer, of course, to clause 70, where the Minister of Finance is asking for power to borrow $10 billion for what he calls public works and general purposes.
I would like to dwell a little on what this government has led us into. The speaker just before me, presumably bucking for a higher role in that caucus, tried to extol the virtues of his government. He took a trip. I take it he stayed at the best hotels in Europe and came away feeling that things are not so bad after all as far as Canada is concerned.
It is the best in Canada.

I hear for the first time this year from one of the Liberals over there, speaking from his seat, who now tells us it is the best. Perhaps that member will listen to a few facts published by no less than the President of the United States in his economic report to Congress. One of the strange facts about this House is that you often find public information available in Washington concerning the performance of this government and its economy that is literally not available here in Canada.
Hear, hear!

Let me point out something to my hon. friend who said he took a trip to Europe and found that things are looking pretty good. Here is what the economic report of the President, transmitted to Congress in January, 1979, has to say about Canada in relation to those European countries.
In table 33 of the report, the annual growth in gross national product per employed worker in major industrial countries is reviewed for the years 1964 to 1978. I am pleased that you are seated, Mr. Speaker, because you are going to be stunned when you hear these figures.
In Japan the real growth between 1964 and 1973 per employed worker was 8.9 per cent. Guess what it was in Canada; 2.4 per cent. In Germany in the same period it was 4.7 per cent, in France 4.5 per cent, in the United Kingdom that this government almost likes to laugh at, 3.2 per cent, and in Italy, 5.4 per cent. Every one of those European countries produced better real growth per worker than Canada.
